⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that observability manufacturer groundcover Inc.
  • According to recent reports, agent Investigations is aimed at the problem of scattered findings as AI agents take on a bigger role in incident response.
  • Investigations in the new workspace are started automatically by groundcover once a monitor issue opens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Industry observers note that observability manufacturer groundcover Inc. today announced the launch of Agent Investigations, a shared workspace designed to allow groundcover’s artificial intelligence agents, a team’s own coding agents and on-call engineers to work production incidents together.

According to recent reports, agent Investigations is aimed at the problem of scattered findings as AI agents take on a bigger role in incident response. When production goes down, several engineers often point their own agents at the same glitch, with each agent working in isolation, according to the organization. What those agents conclude, it says, is end up in private chats, tickets or Slack messages out of view of the rest of the team.

Investigations in the new workspace are started automatically by groundcover once a monitor issue opens. Engineers also have the option to launch one manually from the groundcover interface or from a button in Slack.

On groundcover’s side, the work is split between two agents. The first, known as the Investigator agent, is mentioned to build a graph of questions and hypotheses before testing each one against groundcover’s logs, metrics, traces and Kubernetes data. Supporting graphs are attached to each of its findings.

Reviewing every proposed conclusion is the job of the second, a Moderator agent. The Moderator, which is the only agent allowed to close a hypothesis, sends back any claim that lacks supporting findings. Doing so is remarked to separate generating a possible explanation from validating whether the evidence actually supports it.

Recent findings suggest that ending each hypothesis is a structured assessment that either supports or refutes it. The firm claims teams get a set of tested answers to read through instead of pages of generated text.

Agent Investigations also offers access for outside agents, including Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex, through groundcover’s Model Context Protocol server. Connected agents can read from and contribute to the same investigation, with agents used for business intelligence and product roadmapping also able to take part. In October, groundcover launched agent-to-agent observability tools that let outside coding agents hand production investigations to its own agent.

It has been revealed that hypothesis status and assessments post to the Slack thread tied to the original alert. With replies posted in that thread also fed back into the investigation, engineers are able to steer the work from inside the incident conversation.

Industry observers note that “Every engineer now has an agent, but each of those agents investigates on its own and findings end up in a chat window,” noted co-founder and Chief Executive Shahar Azulay, who started groundcover in 2021 with Yechezkel Rabinovich. “Agent Investigations gives humans and agents one place to work an incident, where every hypothesis is tested against production data and every conclusion has to be backed by evidence.”.

Omer Mayer, senior product manager at groundcover, said the wait while agents are working and the on-call engineer has nothing to look at is often “the hardest stretch of an incident.” Engineers using Agent Investigations instead get to watch, he said, as each hypothesis is supported or ruled out in real time.

In a recent development, the graph the Investigator builds also serves as the record, said to show how a team reached the root cause, including the hypotheses that were ruled out along the way. According to the manufacturer, keeping the monitor, Slack thread, investigation and conclusion linked means nobody has to piece the history back together from separate tools after an incident closes.

Powering the investigations is the full-fidelity telemetry collected by groundcover’s sensor. Because groundcover uses a bring-your-own-cloud architecture, the data remains in the customer’s own cloud account even while agents are querying it.

Sources indicate that agent Investigations is available to groundcover customers whose backends have AI enabled. The organization will demonstrate it at Amazon Web Services Inc.’s re:Invent conference in Las Vegas Nov. 30-Dec. 4.

Groundcover has raised $160 million to date, including a $100 million Series C round led by One Peak in July.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yi He, the co-founder of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has sparked discussions across the crypto market after urging retail traders to stay calm even as major crypto assets continue to post massive daily losses.

Yi He’s consoling statement has come as crypto traders grow increasingly weary and the prolonged market volatility begins to cause even bigger losses, with Bitcoin retesting $63,000.

In her post, Yi urged investors holding major crypto assets that have been substantially affected by the severe market volatility to remain calm amid the latest market downturn.

She described the ongoing crypto market pullback as ‘temporary’ while assuring spot traders that they have little reason to worry.

Alongside the post, Yi He shared a link to the Binance app showcasing a 30-day asset change of approximately -$101.31 million in her account.

The figure indicates the amount of losses the pro-crypto investor has suffered on her holdings over a period of about a month, from October 17 to November 16, 2026.

Although the showcased portfolio indicates a decline in the founder’s holdings, it does not establish whether the decline represents realized trading losses, unrealized losses, withdrawals, or other changes in Yi He’s account.

It appears that some investors may have found comfort in Yi He's message as they expressed support, noting that turbulent conditions like these don’t necessarily last long.

However, other commentators have questioned whether wealthy industry figures like Yi He can fully understand the financial pressure facing retail traders at a time like this.

Some of the arguments questioned how meaningful such reassurance could be for retail investors, arguing that losing 100 million yuan might not significantly affect someone with substantial wealth like her.

Meanwhile, a loss of 20,000 or 30,000 yuan could wipe out an ordinary investor's savings.

#6586. Breaking: Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1131 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.
  • I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.
  • We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

It has been revealed that I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

It has been revealed that most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

According to recent reports, for years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

In a recent development, not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

What I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

According to recent reports, once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:.

In a recent development, “Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”.

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a new closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five housing and mortgage industry trade groups are asking the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to delay a planned increase in condominium association reserve requirements by one year, citing implementation challenges and potential financing disruptions.
  • 19 letter sent to FHFA Director Bill Pulte, the organizations asked the agency to direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to postpone the changes from Jan.
  • The new requirement would increase the minimum reserve allocation for applicable condominium project reviews from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five housing and mortgage industry trade groups are asking the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to delay a planned increase in condominium association reserve requirements by one year, citing implementation challenges and potential financing disruptions.

In a Nov. 19 letter sent to FHFA Director Bill Pulte, the organizations asked the agency to direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to postpone the changes from Jan. 4, 2027, to Jan. 4, 2028.

The new requirement would increase the minimum reserve allocation for applicable condominium project reviews from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income.

The letter was signed by the Community Associations Institute, Community Association Roundtable, Community Home Lenders of America (CHLA), Housing Policy Council and National Association of Mortgage Brokers (NAMB).

The groups remarked they support adequately funded condominium reserves but argued that associations, lenders and homeowners need more time to prepare for the change.

Some have asked for change before. In June, NAMB asked the FHFA to delay upcoming Fannie and Freddie condo review and insurance standards by 12 months. But Fannie Mae retired its limited review process for condominium projects on Aug. 3.

“Condominium project eligibility has already declined following recent changes to project review requirements, including the elimination of Limited Review options,” the groups wrote.

The coalition identified three primary concerns with the planned increase, stating that “the change could have unintended consequences for condominium financing and housing availability.”.

First, many condominium associations operate on annual budget cycles and cannot easily adjust their funding midyear. Some may also need updated reserve studies, board approvals or homeowner consultations before changing their funding practices.

The groups also mentioned questions remain about how the latest requirement will apply to existing budgets, recently completed reserve studies, major capital improvement projects and alternative funding arrangements.

Lenders, servicers and condo management companies will also need time to upgrade their systems, underwriting procedures and project reviews.

Second, the groups warned that associations unable to meet the higher reserve requirement or qualify under an alternative reserve study provision could lose eligibility for conventional financing through the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs). The groups raised concerns that this could reduce the pool of potential buyers, make it more difficult for existing homeowners to sell or refinance, and put pressure on condo resale values.

The impact could be particularly pronounced in older buildings, smaller communities and associations with more “modest-income” homeowners, the letter stated. Projects that lose conventional financing eligibility could become more reliant on nonagency or portfolio loans, which may be more expensive or less readily available.

Lastly, the coalition remarked higher reserve contributions could add to housing costs at a time when homeowners are already facing elevated mortgage payments, property taxes, insurance premiums, maintenance expenses and association fees.

Fannie Mae has estimated that the higher reserve requirement could add an average of $13 to $14 per month to condominium owners’ costs, but the actual increase would vary by association, according to the coalition. Its accompanying analysis illustrated how the additional five percentage points could affect homeowners if the entire increase were funded through regular assessments.

As part of the proposed one-year extension, the coalition urged FHFA to convene industry stakeholders to evaluate the financial and operational effects of the change, clarify how existing reserve studies and funding arrangements will be treated, and develop transition provisions for associations working toward adequate reserve funding.

“We believe that strengthening condominium financial health and maintaining housing affordability should be complementary objectives,” the letter mentioned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.

It has been revealed that upgrade, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Revision, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA noted Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle firm’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan releases that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as promptly as possible.

Amazon Leo noted in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term aims for Vulcan.”.

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

ULA mentioned Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation demonstrated the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t remarked what caused the shortfall.

Sources indicate that impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 debuts reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

It has been revealed that in June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Recent findings suggest that amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security debuts after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the Upcoming Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

Industry observers note that ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

Recent findings suggest that solana has officially removed the "beta" tag from its mainnet's name and introduced the Solana 1.0 standard. The switch was confirmed on Nov. 16 at the Breakpoint conference in London.

"Solana 1.0 marks the network's graduation from 'mainnet beta' to 'mainnet,' retiring the beta designation it has carried since launch," the Solana Foundation mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that solana introduced on March 16, 2020, and the network had been working under the "mainnet-beta" label for six years and eight months. According to the foundation, the label "never evolved to signal its production status.".

According to recent reports, the Solana Foundation coordinated the rollout with the Anza and Firedancer teams. Co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko replied to the announcement on X with three exploding-head emojis.

It has been revealed that "For users, this is the same network, nothing changes. Your SOL, accounts, assets, applications, and transaction history remain the same," the foundation wrote. On Monday, SOL is trading at $71.35.

Industry observers note that according to the foundation, two upgrades made the change possible. In October, Solana activated Alpenglow with the Agave 4.3 release, and the time to final confirmation went down by almost 99%, from 12.8 seconds to around 150 milliseconds.

Firedancer, a validator client developed by Jump Crypto independently from Agave, is also now running on the Solana mainnet. Independent implementations "limit the impact of bugs affecting one client, and strengthen network resilience," the foundation said.

Solana 1.0 also gives the network a shared protocol version, and it does not depend on the version numbers of individual clients such as Agave and Firedancer.

In a recent development, "A shared protocol version lets everyone refer to Solana's evolution without using one client's release number as shorthand for the entire network," the Solana Foundation explained. "Announcing a protocol version does not activate every associated improvement at once.".

Earlier this year, Solana raised the compute limit per block from 60 million to 100 million compute units in May, and the slot time went down from 400 to 200 milliseconds in August. The maximum transaction size also went up from 1,232 to 4,096 bytes.

"Documentation, websites, explorers, and other ecosystem surfaces will progressively reflect the updated designation," the foundation added.

It has been revealed that deployment services are becoming the real battleground in AI infrastructure as buyers discover that shipping hardware is only half the job. With GPU supply tight and refresh cycles accelerating, neoclouds and enterprises are judging suppliers on how promptly an AI factory actually goes live.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s not just enough to deliver to the customers. They want it online as promptly as possible. Time is money,” Thauberger said.

Thauberger spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how deployment services are driving the race to time to online and how liquid cooling retrofits help older facilities take on modern AI racks. (* Disclosure below.).

Customers are leaning on suppliers for far more than boxes. Allocation and deployment services are the two biggest requests Supermicro hears, and its service teams bring systems up, run customer workloads and hand off only once everything is running, Thauberger explained.

It has been revealed that “We know that we’re in a constrained environment. There’s no secret on that. So customers are basically asking Supermicro how quickly you can get allocation, how quickly you can bring it online, and how quickly you can have people out on site to deploy those,” Thauberger said.

In a recent development, older facilities pose another hurdle. Many weren’t designed for the liquid cooling and power density of modern AI racks, so Supermicro offers retrofit options such as sidecars and in-row coolant distribution units, according to Thauberger. The company has also added pre-assembled AI racks to its building-block lineup to shorten installs.

“We have the largest liquid cooling capacity based in California. We’re a U.S.-headquartered manufacturer, and the ability for us to have as much liquid cooling capacity as we have inside the U.S. allows us to deploy to these AI factories quick inside the United States,” Thauberger remarked.

#6578. A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it.
  • Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.
  • when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he stated.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A major part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively fresh sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he mentioned, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

Sources indicate that what you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he mentioned.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that and when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré remarked; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

It has been revealed that the CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

According to recent reports, bitcoin price is getting hammered in the aftermath of the FOMC minutes. Gold isn’t doing much better; oil and stocks have joined the sell-off. The markets are already nervous about the Federal Reserve’s next decision, and yesterday’s FOMC minutes gave us another reason to worry: policymakers are still talking about raising interest rates.

It has been revealed that almost all officials saw further hikes as appropriate under their baseline outlook. Two even floated the possibility of a bigger increase if inflation refuses to cool.

This is a nasty combination for markets. Bitcoin fell around 3.2% over 24 hours, gold futures dropped more than 3%, and WTI crude lost around 3%. The dollar climbed to a 19-month high. Wall Street was mixed, though, with the Nasdaq finishing higher while the Dow and S&P 500 slipped.

In a recent development, here’s the comparison. In March 2020, the Fed was slashing rates, buying bonds and throwing emergency liquidity at a financial system under immense pressure. Congress approved a $2.2 trillion rescue package to keep households and businesses afloat.

Today, we are watching markets fall while the Fed is possibly making money more expensive.

October’s FOMC minutes weren’t exactly what markets wanted to hear. The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4% during its October meeting, but almost all participants believed further increases would likely be appropriate. Two officials also stated a hike larger than the usual 25 basis points could be considered if inflation data came in hotter than expected.

And there was more in those minutes than just interest rates. Officials raised concerns about hedge fund leverage and the growing debt tied to artificial intelligence investments. Some financing arrangements could become a problem if investors start questioning enormous AI spending, and whether it will generate the returns companies expect.

According to recent reports, the risk is forced selling. Leveraged funds facing losses or investor withdrawals may have to dump assets promptly, potentially pushing prices down further.

Gold has its own problem. A stronger dollar and higher interest rates make it less attractive to investors who can earn a return elsewhere. Bitcoin price, meanwhile, remains vulnerable when traders cut exposure to speculative assets.

The Fed hasn’t declared a financial emergency. Its minutes actually describe the banking system as resilient. But officials are clearly paying attention to risks that could amplify a market shock.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

March 2020 was brutal. COVID-19 lockdowns brought businesses to a standstill. Investors rushed for cash, stocks collapsed, and Bitcoin briefly slipped below $4,000 after sitting near $10,000 just weeks earlier.

The Federal Reserve didn’t wait around. It cut rates by 50 basis points on March 3, then delivered another 100-basis-point cut on March 15. The federal funds target range dropped to 0%–0.25%.

According to recent reports, on March 23, the Fed announced unlimited purchases of Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities, promising to buy whatever amounts were necessary to support market functioning. It also introduced emergency lending programmes to keep credit flowing.

President Donald Trump signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act on March 27. The package included direct payments to eligible Americans, expanded unemployment benefits, and assistance for businesses struggling to survive lockdowns. The Paycheck Protection Program gave small businesses access to loans designed to help them keep employees on payroll.

In a recent development, the response was enormous, but the economy was facing an extraordinary shutdown. Millions of Americans had lost their jobs, businesses were closing, and normal economic activity had practically disappeared.

Industry observers note that markets eventually bounced back. The S&P 500 recovered its pre-pandemic record by August 2020. Bitcoin climbed above $12,000 during the same month.

Sources indicate that the current US economy isn’t in the same position as it was during the pandemic. Inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target, and policymakers are discussing rate increases rather than cuts.

According to recent reports, slashing rates to zero and flooding markets with liquidity might help asset prices. It could also make inflation worse. Another multitrillion-dollar spending package would face an entirely different argument in Congress, especially without a pandemic-style economic shutdown.

It has been revealed that the Fed doesn’t have to choose between doing nothing and repeating the 2020 rescue. If banks struggle to fund themselves or credit markets start freezing, it can step in with emergency lending and liquidity operations. That’s a much narrower response than another round of unlimited bond purchases.

Recent findings suggest that the Fed’s concerns about leveraged hedge funds and AI financing could become more relevant if investors start selling indiscriminately. A market correction is one thing. Forced selling spreading through the financial system is another.

At the moment, there’s no evidence that we’re facing another March 2020. The banking system remains resilient, and falling Bitcoin prices alone won’t trigger a government bailout.

Recent findings suggest that but the Fed has a problem that didn’t exist in quite the same way during the pandemic. It may need to protect financial stability without giving up its fight against inflation. In 2020, Washington opened the taps. This time, we wait and see, and Bitcoin price will survive.

Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy, spent $228.1 million buying back its STRC preferred stock between Nov. 9 and Nov. 15, according to the company's fresh filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Over the same period, Strategy bought 485 BTC for $33.4 million, so the company spent almost seven times more on STRC than on Bitcoin.

In a recent development, "Strategy has acquired 485 BTC and repurchased $228M of STRC. As of 11/15/26, we hold 850,849 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets," Michael Saylor wrote on X.

Sources indicate that the filing shows that Strategy sold 2.09 million shares of its Class A common stock and raised $244.7 million. The organization used $206.3 million of that amount for STRC buybacks and added another $21.8 million from interest earned on its dollar reserves.

According to recent reports, the 485 BTC were bought at an average price of $68,887 per coin. The remaining $5 million from the share sales stayed on the books as free cash.

STRC, also known as Stretch, is a perpetual preferred stock with a variable monthly dividend, and Strategy launched it in July 2025.

When the price of Bitcoin slipped below $65,000, STRC fell to $99.08. Strategy aims to keep STRC close to its $100 par value, and the company has another $332.2 million set aside for buybacks. The board of Strategy also approved a December STRC dividend at an annual rate of 12%, or $1.00 per share.

"USD Duration is 3.4 yrs and STRC's BTC Credit tightened to 67 bps (-3 bps), assuming 10% BTC ARR, 40% BTC Vol, and a BTC price of $68,800," Saylor added.

As of Nov. 15, Strategy held 850,849 BTC, bought for a total of $64.2 billion at an average price of $75,452 per coin. On Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $63,941, and Strategy's holdings are worth around $54.4 billion.

In a recent development, the unrealized loss of the firm on its Bitcoin holdings stands at around $9.8 billion. On Sunday, when the price of Bitcoin fell to $62,029 on Bitfinex, the loss was above $11 billion.

Strategy also holds $4.9 billion in dollar assets, and $4.75 billion of that amount is in its dedicated USD reserve.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (836 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am.
  • Sources indicate that it’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows.
  • These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a latest OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am.

Sources indicate that it’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a latest OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows consumers are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”.

Instead, the Copilot as “a new OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Sources indicate that microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

Industry observers note that the high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

It has been revealed that operating systems like Windows provide customers with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The Upcoming OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Recent findings suggest that at the moment, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the fresh Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as Fresh OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, people don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

According to recent reports, “We increasingly think of all our apps together as a upcoming operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” said Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

In a recent development, the end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella noted.

According to recent reports, the Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

AI’s next build-out: Inference racks that resize themselves for every latest model

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (735 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Memory pooling is fast becoming one of the sharpest tools in AI inference economics, with companies racing to wring more output from every graphics processing unit.
  • Most AI servers still ship with a fixed GPU-to-memory ratio that holds for the life of the machine.
  • Sources indicate that “Our core fundamental technology is around pooling and sharing the most critical resources in the data center, which are now GPU and memory,” Puri remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:43 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Memory pooling is fast becoming one of the sharpest tools in AI inference economics, with companies racing to wring more output from every graphics processing unit.

Most AI servers still ship with a fixed GPU-to-memory ratio that holds for the life of the machine. But that is a poor fit when nobody knows what model they will deploy six months from now, according to Sumit Puri (pictured), co-founder and chief technical officer of Liqid Inc.

Sources indicate that “Our core fundamental technology is around pooling and sharing the most critical resources in the data center, which are now GPU and memory,” Puri remarked. “Rather than statically deploying these things inside of a server, our vision is simple. Let’s put pools of resources in the rack, GPUs and memory, and dynamically assign them to any server that needs it based upon the model or the workload that we are looking to deploy.”.

Sources indicate that puri spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed pooling GPUs and memory, the tokenomics of AI inference and Liqid as a Service. (* Disclosure below.).

Sources indicate that liqid measures payoff in tokenomics, with the yardsticks being tokens per second, tokens per watt and, above all, tokens per dollar. Supply is another pressure point in the AI infrastructure build-out, with memory among its most constrained components. But delivering only the memory each application needs stretches scarce supply further, Puri explained.

“Supply chain is a massive constraint for all of us — memory being a giantly massive constrained thing,” he remarked. “If we can do things like pool memory, share memory, optimally deliver memory to the server in the right amount of memory as required by the application, we can directly address some of those supply chain challenges.”.

In a recent development, liqid is also widening how customers buy memory pooling. At SC26, the company announced Liqid as a Service, a fully managed, single-tenant offering, and it is moving toward preconfigured appliances. The bet is that most enterprises will deploy models rather than build them and therefore require their own capacity, according to Puri.

Recent findings suggest that “The world went to unlimited consumption of minutes, and that’s where we believe tokens are headed,” Puri stated. “Everybody’s going to own their own token machine so they can consume these tokens at will.”.

#6572. Why some regional brokerages are avoiding ancillary services

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1402 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Why some regional brokerages are avoiding ancillary services

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1402 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • housing market may see fewer than 4 million existing home sales in 2027.
  • From fresh mortgage joint ventures to diving into mortgage servicing, companies from eXp Realty to HomeServices of America are looking to further integrate the disparate parts of a real estate transaction into one vertical platform.
  • “Our firm has been around for 153 years and our strategy has always been to be masters of our craft and not to chase every adjacent revenue stream,” Matt Leone, the chief marketing officer at Brown Harris Stevens (BHS), a RealTrends Verified brokerage, said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s no secret that the U.S. housing market may see fewer than 4 million existing home sales in 2027. In an attempt to boost ever-tightening margins and claim a larger slice of the transaction pie, many large national brokerages have spent the past year doubling down on ancillary services.

From fresh mortgage joint ventures to diving into mortgage servicing, companies from eXp Realty to HomeServices of America are looking to further integrate the disparate parts of a real estate transaction into one vertical platform. While this may be the way some of the nation’s largest brokerage companies are thinking about the future, many regional brokerages with strong market share in their states or metros are taking a different tack.

“Our firm has been around for 153 years and our strategy has always been to be masters of our craft and not to chase every adjacent revenue stream,” Matt Leone, the chief marketing officer at Brown Harris Stevens (BHS), a RealTrends Verified brokerage, said. “I think that we are a residential resale, new development and property management brokerage. Mortgage and title may offer additional income, but our greatest opportunity is to stay relentlessly focused on real estate and be the best at that. I think, when you venture into other arenas, your core gets saturated and your eyes come off the prize.”.

Like BHS, Linda O’Koniewski’s RealTrends Verified firm, Leading Edge Real Estate, is also staying out of ancillary services.

Sources indicate that “While margins are critically thin for brokerages, and the income would be welcome, we have given it all up,” O’Koniewski mentioned, noting that her company had previously had partnerships with insurance and mortgage companies. “What our clients need is the best loan officer and product. They need a super-responsive insurance agent. We are dedicating ourselves to developing processes and strategies that pre-resolve preventable problems in a transaction and create the best outcomes for our clients.”.

O’Koniewski added that her firm’s in-house legal counsel has also suggested homing in on real estate as industries like mortgage and title are not their primary area of expertise.

Although firms like Leading Edge and BHS may not own or have ancillary services joint ventures, this doesn’t mean they lack relationships with lenders or title companies.

At BHS, instead of offering mortgage or title services directly or through a joint venture, the tech giant works with trusted mortgage or title professionals to contribute to the company’s blog, sponsor its podcasts and participate in educational panel discussions.

Leone remarked BHS works to establish relationships with the top mortgage and title professionals through a “massive in-house commitment to marketing and content creation,” bringing voices from ancillary services industries that BHS feels are the most aligned with its culture and mission.

“They’re providing their expertise to our audience that follows us, as well as providing advertising support to expand the audience that views our 18-plus podcasts and in-house created episodic series shows,” he said. “It is legitimate advertising and earned media exposure at fair market value that allows us to get their expertise to broadcast that to our client base and it also allows us to have an ancillary source of legitimate income.”.

Through these posts and marketing material, Leone stated BHS is looking to educate its agents and clients, which is why the brokerage likes to partner with creative and experienced ancillary services providers through the program.

“We’re bringing experienced professionals that have seen it all before, and we like to bring those individuals in to get their insights,” Leone said. “Hopefully it allows everyone to stay informed and that is our goal when we’re creating content.”.

While not yet as advanced as BHS’s marketing machine, this is what Peter Voss is looking to do with the in-house video production and editing segment he and his team have debuted at 3% Listing Co.

Recent findings suggest that “Agents can schedule a time with the in-house video team whenever they want and work with our director on a script and then get in front of the camera and record. We take care of all the editing and produce the video,” Voss said.

Voss said, for his firm, the video production started as a way to provide services to their agents that are beneficial to their business, but also something his firm could afford without significantly increasing overhead costs.

“It is a way to help our agents get their branding out and hopefully generate more transactions, which helps them but also helps our business,” he said.

In the future, Voss remarked they are looking to expand this service beyond just 3% Listing Co agents, allowing the firm to have an additional revenue stream similar to BHS’s operation.

It has been revealed that while brokerages like BHS, 3% Listing Co. and Leading Edge may not feel the need to go all-in on ancillary services, Michele Harrington, at First Team Real Estate, a RealTrends Verified firm, sees them as a must-have.

“It is kind of a no-brainer. The profit margins in the real estate brokerage business are just so tiny, so any little bump in the market or a downturn in the market is really going to hurt,” Harrington, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, mentioned.

According to recent reports, this is why Harrington believes anyone who owns a brokerage should be exploring ancillary services. Even prior to opening First Team, Harrington, who previously led a 300-agent firm based in Southern California, had her own escrow and mortgage companies.

At First Team, Harrington runs an escrow firm and a mortgage brokerage operation. She previously had mortgage joint ventures, but said she preferred going the owned mortgage operation route in order to maximize margins.

According to recent reports, “The joint venture business isn’t my favorite type of mortgage operation because it is hard to be competitive and have good rates for consumers when everyone involved is trying to make a profit,” she stated. “So, your best bet is being a broker where you can go directly to the banks or Rocket or United Wholesale Mortgage and broker the loan. It makes you way more competitive.”.

By owning ancillary services, not only can you boost your profit margins, Harrington also feels it enables brokers to provide even better service to consumers.

Industry observers note that “It gives you more control. If something goes wrong with escrow or mortgage, the agent calls me, and I tell the president that they need to fix it. That level of control is a nice perk for the agents,” Harrington remarked.

Beyond providing her agents with more control over transactions, Harrington said having ancillary businesses within her organization also helps First Team be more competitive as a brokerage.

“If I want to be more competitive in my splits or be more competitive by offering signing bonuses, I can do those things because ancillary services increase my margins,” she noted.

While Voss sees the value of having ancillary services operations, especially when it comes to revenue opportunities, he still doesn’t believe the juice is necessarily worth the squeeze.

Sources indicate that “We have talked about bringing mortgage in-house, but what we have found is that in-house operations can be a turn off to a lot of agents,” Voss stated. “They feel like it is kind of forced on them to have to send their clients to their firm’s mortgage lender. We are really focused on recruitment right now, so that is why we have shied away from this.”.

Leone agrees, telling HousingWire that in-house mortgage or title operations often feel like a “forced option” that agents have to suggest to their clients.

It has been revealed that “We don’t want to get in between the relationship of the client and our agent and the agents understand who is best for their client and who is best for that transaction,” he remarked. “Different lenders make sense for different neighborhoods, price points and scenarios and we don’t want to get in the middle of that.”.

Instead Leone and Voss feel that their companies can generate more revenue by focusing on being the best at helping buyers and sellers transact real estate.

“We really focus on our relationships with mortgage lenders and title companies and making sure that we make their jobs easier so that they may be more open to sending business to us and our agents because they know we will get the job done,” Voss said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Authorities in the United States and Canada have declared a major cross-border crackdown on cryptocurrency fraud, bringing together law enforcement agencies, financial regulators and private companies to target online scam networks.

Industry observers note that the Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) announced on Nov. 16 the launch of Operation Niagara, a coordinated initiative aimed at disrupting organized cryptocurrency fraud schemes and protecting potential victims.

According to the Canadian securities regulator, the operation involves investigators, securities specialists and financial crime experts from both countries.

The initiative will use advanced technology and enhanced investigative capabilities to identify fraudulent activity and potential victims in near real time.

Importantly, the operation will not focus solely on investigating criminals after fraud has occurred. Authorities also intend to identify individuals who are being targeted by scammers and intervene before they suffer further financial losses.

"Fraud knows no border, and it targets everyday people," said Bonnie Lysyk, Executive Vice-President of Enforcement at the OSC.

Recent findings suggest that the initiative brings together several major law enforcement and regulatory agencies, including the U.S. Secret Service, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) and Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).

Canadian securities regulators, including the Alberta Securities Commission, British Columbia Securities Commission and Autorité des marchés financiers, are also participating.

Private-sector companies will contribute technical expertise and intelligence to help authorities identify and disrupt fraudulent networks.

It’s worth noting that the OSC didn’t provide details on how many fraud networks it is targeting, how many potential victims have been identified or how much cryptocurrency is involved in Operation Niagara.

#6570. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (829 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that want to price more precisely?
  • When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

In a recent development, A sold comp tells us where a buyer remarked yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

In a recent development, imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Industry observers note that suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

In a recent development, when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Sources indicate that maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Sources indicate that listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

It has been revealed that so, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

It has been revealed that “I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Sources indicate that twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

According to recent reports, find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sources indicate that sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 11:38 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

The neocloud boom is entering a sorting phase, and global cloud availability is emerging as the line between providers built for enterprise AI and those built to rent out racks of graphics processing units.

Recent findings suggest that with agentic AI moving from pilots into production, buyers are looking past raw GPU counts toward integrated platforms they can build on. That shift is redrawing the competitive map for cloud AI infrastructure. Enterprise practitioners are now starting ambitious agentic AI agendas, and they need the full stack of services behind AI-native applications rather than standalone clusters, according to Kevin Cochrane (pictured, right), chief marketing officer of Vultr.

In a recent development, “There are those providers that are trusted platforms, that are global cloud platforms that have the totality of services that are required for real agentic AI deployments,” Cochrane said. “We’ll continue to see a separation of the pack and there’ll be those that are trusted platforms that enterprises can rely on and there’ll be those that aren’t.”.

It has been revealed that cochrane and Duncan Ng (left), vice president of solutions engineering at Vultr, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why agentic AI is reviving demand for central processing units, how Vultr builds data centers as integrated systems and which neocloud providers are likely to survive consolidation. (* Disclosure below.).

Sources indicate that calling a service an enterprise cloud takes more than racking accelerators. Vultr organizes its footprint into data center regions, each of which can control multiple facilities on one network. Developers get one application programming interface they can hook into a Terraform template, Cochrane explained. Many rivals, by contrast, stood up individual sites quickly to serve bespoke customer contracts.

Recent findings suggest that “In traditional neoclouds, the data centers are actually islands. They’re not connected. It’s not one unified global network. It’s not one unified global platform,” Cochrane mentioned. “These are like individual data centers stood up very quickly for bespoke customer contract. That is not a platform.”.

Agentic AI is also reshaping the hardware mix inside those regions. Reasoning models now let agents chain dozens of steps, call tools and validate results in flight — work that leans heavily on CPUs, according to Ng. Vultr ran a cloud for more than a decade before the GPU rush and has used processors from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. as the backbone of its CPU fleet for several years, he added. The firm has since extended that partnership to accelerators with a $1.2 billion order for AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems.

Sources indicate that “This increased density, this increased usage — these are just new hosting companies,” Ng said. “This is just a new application that is 10 times more compute dense than the last that we’re trying to sell to.”.

Industry observers note that enterprises are finally moving those workloads out of pilot and into production, Ng noted. One Massive Four global systems integrator uses Vultr as the substrate for a risk management service. Vultr has been rolling out platform upgrades aimed at enterprise agentic AI to support that kind of deployment.

According to recent reports, “What they’re doing is something that used to take consulting hours, people poring through spreadsheets and poring through invoices, poring through declarations,” he noted. “They now are able to automate significant portions of this to serve a larger number of their customers and do a deeper dive into their risk supply chains.”.
