Breaking: New CEO at Villa eyes manufactured housing, ADU opportunity

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Offsite construction, one of the housing affordability crisis’s hidden-in-plain-sight solutions, gained a blast of momentum this summer when the ROAD Act called for removing the permanent chassis requirement for manufactured homes.
  • Villa, which operates in California and Colorado, is among them.
  • Since launching in 2019, the tech giant has delivered more than 425 homes across three core verticals: manufactured single-family communities, ADUs on single-family lots, and ADUs within multifamily communities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Offsite construction, one of the housing affordability crisis’s hidden-in-plain-sight solutions, gained a blast of momentum this summer when the ROAD Act called for removing the permanent chassis requirement for manufactured homes. Now, some builders are preparing to capitalize on that growing buzz.

Villa, which operates in California and Colorado, is among them.

Since launching in 2019, the tech giant has delivered more than 425 homes across three core verticals: manufactured single-family communities, ADUs on single-family lots, and ADUs within multifamily communities.

The builder originally focused exclusively on ADUs, but has since expanded into primary homes, delivering its first batch of manufactured single-family houses in Northern California earlier this year. The organization is right now building 25 homes in Santa Rosa, California and 14 duplexes in Westminster, Colorado, while also helping rebuild housing for victims of the 2025 Eaton Fire in Altadena, California.

According to recent reports, the goal now is to scale both the ADU and manufactured housing businesses, with intends for larger single-family communities of up to about 100 lots. To support that growth, Villa declared earlier this week that it hired David Messenger, former CFO of Century Communities, as its next CEO.

For Messenger, moving from one of the country’s largest production homebuilders to an offsite builder focused on ADUs and infill development is quite a pivot. But it also represents an opportunity to focus more on attainable housing in the high-cost areas where Villa operates.

Industry observers note that for example, in Santa Rosa, a city of about 180,000 north of San Francisco, the average home price is about $705,000. Comparatively, homes in Villa’s upcoming community, Acacia Village, start at $620,000.

“I’ve been drawn to affordable, attainable housing. I think it’s something that the country needs,” Messenger said in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

Beyond the opportunity to deliver attainable housing where it’s badly needed, Messenger sees room for growth across all of Villa’s verticals.

According to recent reports, “We’ve got three verticals already established. I think all three can continue to grow,” he stated.

Villa’s ADU business has plenty of room to grow, Messenger said. Homeowners in California and Colorado are driving strong and growing demand, while California multifamily operators are increasingly building ADUs on open or underutilized land to generate extra rental income.

“More and more multifamily operators see [ADUs] as a way to increase their rental income…at a relatively low cost to their overall project,” Messenger mentioned.

According to recent reports, the other growth opportunity is in Villa’s new manufactured home communities. Messenger sees an opening to partner with land developers to build larger communities, potentially with up to around 100 lots. Instead of taking on the expense and risk of acquiring, entitling and developing land themselves, Villa plans to purchase fully entitled and developed land.

“There is an opportunity to work with land developers who, as they’re developing land, are looking for a takeout. The land developers don’t necessarily want to own the land long term. I think if we can provide them a takeout when it’s finished, that is an attractive option for both of us, as we can buy a finished lot. I don’t think that Villa is going to be in the game of developing land, and we’re not looking to take on entitlement risk,” Messenger explained.

According to recent reports, messenger also intends to draw on his experience at Century Communities to help Villa build a more scalable operation. Although the companies operate differently, he believes many of the same production homebuilding principles can apply.

According to recent reports, “Having spent 10 years at a production homebuilder, you learn how to establish repeatable processes. Homebuilding involves unpredictable issues every day, so the goal is to make those issues more predictable. Offsite construction lends itself to that because a significant portion of the home is built in a factory, making the process more predictable. It’s about establishing standardized processes that can be repeated for every unit and every lot,” Messenger said.

“Once we get those processes working like a machine, that’s what makes the business scalable,” he added.

Recent findings suggest that as Villa scales, Messenger doesn’t expect production capacity to be an glitch. Instead of owning and operating its own factories, the manufacturer contracts with reputable, third-party production facilities to build its homes and ADUs.

“We’ve partnered with different factories all over the state of California. We partner with factories in Colorado, Nebraska and Albuquerque for dealing with those projects. We are developing an extensive array of relationships to make sure that we don’t get hamstrung by a capacity problem,” he noted.

Industry observers note that the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law in July, included a provision that removed the decades-long requirement that manufactured homes be built with a permanent steel chassis. The change has received a lot of attention, leading The Fresh York Times to name chassis as its word of the day on November 11.

Manufacturers cite two main benefits of this rule change, which the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development is now finalizing. First, removing the steel chassis gives manufactured homebuilders greater design flexibility, allowing them to build larger, multi-story and more aesthetically appealing homes that more closely resemble traditional site-built housing.

“If you actually walk through a manufactured home product today and look at the finishes being delivered, it’s a completely different product from what people actually think about. If we can do some marketing and outreach and get people in the door to see what these homes look like, I think they’ll be amazed at what they see,” Messenger said.

That added design flexibility could help the industry shed longstanding stigmas and gain acceptance in communities where zoning restrictions historically thwarted manufactured housing, which is typically a more affordable alternative to traditional stick-built homes.

Manufacturers also see an opportunity to expand into high-cost urban and suburban infill markets, where multi-story designs can make higher-density development more economically feasible. Villa, which operates in high-cost cities with limited developable land, is among the homebuilders positioned to benefit from this rule change.

“As we’re evaluating communities, not having a chassis requirement should open up more lots and communities where we can build on,” Messenger remarked. “I think it provides additional opportunities for us.”.

#6564. What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am.
  • Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.
  • That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am.

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft states active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the company posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

It has been revealed that microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

Recent findings suggest that that’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

When traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:.

Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

Recent findings suggest that the company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that the safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate matter,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

The gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

According to recent reports, teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the firm put it, so email stayed down.

Microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that was months old.

The company’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Sources indicate that charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Microsoft notes it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put latest limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

It has been revealed that it may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate problem,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t said what it was.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • Recent findings suggest that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

Recent findings suggest that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

According to recent reports, “Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont stated in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon noted in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

Recent findings suggest that the terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

In a recent development, “Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an notable step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

Industry observers note that “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s crucial to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

It has been revealed that “A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really vital component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker stated. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

Recent findings suggest that fundstrat co-founder and BitMine chairman Tom Lee expects the price of Ethereum to bottom shortly before the Nasdaq debut of Anthropic. "If ETH follows the same path as the SPCX IPO, ETH bottoms shortly before the ANT IPO," Lee wrote on X.

Lee shared a Bloomberg and Fundstrat chart that compares the price of ETH ahead of the SpaceX IPO in June with the current decline. According to the chart, ETH lost 39% over eight weeks before the SpaceX offering, including 29% in the final two weeks. Ahead of the Anthropic IPO, ETH has also lost 39% over two months, including 28% in the last two weeks.

If ETH follows same path as SPCX IPO, $ETH bottoms shortly before $ANT IPO https://t.co/FS6T3KiRpo.

SpaceX raised a record $75 billion in its IPO in June. The bottom for ETH came three trading days before SpaceX priced its shares, and the price of ETH went up after that.

It has been revealed that anthropic is set to price its IPO on Nov. 18 and aims to raise up to $64.4 billion. It would be the second-largest IPO in history after SpaceX.

It has been revealed that lee blamed the decline of ETH on a rotation of money into the Anthropic IPO, and Binance founder Changpeng Zhao and Strive CEO Matt Cole have pointed to the same flow of liquidity. On Monday, ETH is trading at $1,823.

It has been revealed that bitMine Immersion Technologies (BMNR), which Lee chairs, has bought ETH every week since it launched its treasury strategy on June 30, 2025. In its Nov. 16 patch, the company disclosed fresh numbers: it added 7,653 ETH to its reserves last week and 9,587 ETH the week before.

Sources indicate that bitMine now holds 6,077,745 ETH, or 4.97% of all coins in circulation (about 122.2 million ETH), and it is the world's largest corporate Ethereum treasury. According to the manufacturer, it is 99% of the way through its "Alchemy of 5%" program, and fewer than 35,000 ETH are left to reach the target.

The total portfolio of BitMine, which includes crypto, cash, securities and venture stakes, has shrunk from a peak of more than $14 billion to $11.8 billion. According to BitMine, 5,227,037 ETH, or around 86% of the reserve, is staked.

Lee expects the growth cycle for ETH to last two to three years, driven by bank tokenization, and his base-case targets for ETH range from $12,000 to $22,000.

Tech Report: China-based AI robotics biotech firm MegaRobo raises $200M to accelerate scientific discovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chinese biotech robotics firm MegaRobo Co.
  • Founded in 2016, MegaRobo builds robotic systems that let artificial intelligence software run physical experiments, alongside precision measurement and inspection tools for manufacturers.
  • Investors joining the round included Oman Investment Authority, Asia Investment Capital, Granite Asia, Sinovation Ventures and CMB International.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 11:45 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Chinese biotech robotics firm MegaRobo Co. Ltd. today confirmed it has raised $200 million in new funding to invest in its core technology and expand its automated life sciences infrastructure for increasingly complex physical systems.

Founded in 2016, MegaRobo builds robotic systems that let artificial intelligence software run physical experiments, alongside precision measurement and inspection tools for manufacturers.

Investors joining the round included Oman Investment Authority, Asia Investment Capital, Granite Asia, Sinovation Ventures and CMB International. The organization raised $600 million to date across multiple funding rounds, including nearly $300 million in Series C during 2022.

“The first generation of AI learned from humanity’s accumulated knowledge. The next generation will increasingly learn by acting in the physical world — through experiments, production and continuous feedback,” said founder and Chief Executive Daniel Huang. “That shift changes AI from a system that interprets the world into one that can help create new knowledge, materials, processes and products.”.

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant’s two most prominently marketed offerings are Megalaxy Lab, an AI-connected experimental platform and CellVue T2000, its automated cell-imaging instrument. Both appear on the company’s English-language homepage. MegaRobo also sells more specialized lab equipment, including the Auflo sample-preparation workstation and the Seloris cell culturing automation system.

The key distinction is that Megalaxy Lab is the public face for the firm’s AI-for-science strategy, while CellVue and other systems represent concrete examples of the instruments it builds for the industry.

The company said through Megalaxy it is making real-world experimentation programmable and accessible. Researchers and AI agents can configure experiments, route them through automated laboratory systems, track execution, receive structured, machine-readable results, and feed them directly into the next cycle of scientific reasoning. This includes virtual large data readouts that can be amplified as digital twins representing the scientific data, protein design, biochemistry and other properties.

Sources indicate that megaRobo noted it’s working together with industry partners, including Tencent Cloud and Twist Bioscience, to expand its capability in the AI Science community with the launch of Poreva Open, a global AI protein design challenge open to all models and technical approaches. Megalaxy will provide wet-lab validation for more than 10,000 protein design sequences, creating an opportunity to test models against real experimental data.

Industry observers note that the manufacturer is also developing the One Intelligence Stack as a common technology foundation for instruments, machines, materials processes and real-world feedback. It’s not just a collection of isolated AI applications and products, but a chain infrastructure that enables AI to act, learn and observe across complex physical environments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 16, 2026 at 8:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 8:32 am.
  • Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.
  • The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 16, 2026 at 8:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 8:32 am.

Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he mentioned in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Sources indicate that over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The Fresh York Times. Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Sources indicate that bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

According to recent reports, pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s prepares for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Industry observers note that amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk.

To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, mentioned in a statement. Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson stated. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”.

Some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”.

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post, writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”.

According to recent reports, fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others said the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.

I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She swiftly responded via text.

It has been revealed that “No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”.

  • “In an uncertain environment, you have to initiative and execute to your down case scenarios, and then when something better than down case happens, you’re that much better,” Allen mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With mortgage lenders continuing to cut expenses, including personnel, as the originations forecast for 2027 dims, Jesse Allen said the reverse mortgage business at Rate is still growing and he isn’t waiting for federal housing leaders to offer help.

It has been revealed that at last week’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association Annual Meeting & Expo, Allen said he’s planning for the “down case” on Federal Housing Administration policy regarding upfront mortgage insurance premiums (MIP) for Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs). Allen’s comments came not long after Ginnie Mae President Joe Gormley said the Trump administration is “very comfortable” with current MIP structures for FHA-insured single-family home loans and reverse mortgages.

“In an uncertain environment, you have to initiative and execute to your down case scenarios, and then when something better than down case happens, you’re that much better,” Allen mentioned.

Industry observers note that allen, the president of the 55+ lending division at Rate and a NRMLA board member for 2026-27, sat down with HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily at NRMLA Annual to discuss some of the hot topics of interest for industry professionals. He mentioned that lenders should look to expand their product menus to insulate themselves from any obstacles to federally insured loans, and he pitched responsible home equity release as the next big opportunity for the wider mortgage industry.

NRMLA and other trade groups have spent the past year arguing that the FHA could lower the upfront mortgage insurance premium for certain borrowers. Allen mentioned that cutting some fees would pull more people into the FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, which he called “basic insurance economics.” NRMLA has also laid out the math to lower premiums for borrowers who utilize less of their HECM proceeds while lobbying to eliminate second appraisals.

Recent findings suggest that but with the political transition underway after the recent midterm elections, Allen does not expect quick action. “I’m not building my business model or business case around that,” he remarked. “If positive things happen, it’s wind in the sails.”.

Still, a lower upfront MIP could be “powerful for older homeowners” who want to access their equity responsibly, he mentioned, as they might tap 30% to 40% of their available line of credit now while saving the rest for later in retirement.

When asked whether he thinks a more balanced Congress is coming in 2027, Allen said everyone’s definition of balanced differs. But he also believes that if Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) takes over the Senate banking committee, “we’re going to see more regulatory interest.” Allen’s approach, he added, is to operate daily as though auditors are showing up, which should be the standard for a business that serves a protected class of senior homeowners.

Industry observers note that allen clarified that Rate is a nondelegated correspondent lender for proprietary reverse mortgage products and is fully delegated on FHA-backed HECM products. Proprietary loans make up about 40% of Rate’s reverse mortgage originations, he stated, and he estimated them at 55% to 65% of its volume based on their typically larger loan sizes.

Similar to the industry at large, private-label loans are where growth is happening at Rate, although its HECM volume is rising too, Allen mentioned, with the company outpacing the industry year over year. According to data compiled by Reverse Market Insight, Rate was the 13th-largest HECM lender in the country through the first nine months of the year, with its 228 endorsements up 41% compared to the same period in 2025.

Proprietary loans often serve borrowers that FHA products can’t, including owners of high-value homes and those who want to pay off consumer debt without it counting against them in qualification — a guideline NRMLA has pushed to change. But Allen remarked his team spends time reminding loan officers that the HECM is “still an awesome product.”.

Compared with a traditional home equity line of credit, he said, a HECM line of credit mitigates the risk that falling home values lead to frozen lines, leaving borrowers without access when “they need their equity the most.” HECM lines of credit can grow for the life of the loan if the borrower doesn’t exhaust funds and meets requirements like property tax and insurance payments. Proprietary lines of credit typically stop growing after seven to 10 years, Allen added.

Allen pointed to reverse for purchase financing as a tool for addressing affordability. He stated that one of Rate’s top loan officers recently closed a reverse for purchase for the parent of one of his real estate agent partners. The LO had a couple of reverse mortgages under his belt but had never done a purchase deal, and he worked with one of the firm’s specialists to get it done.

“Specialty lending in general is a substantial priority for most mortgage companies today,” Allen remarked, naming non-QM and builder programs alongside reverse.

According to recent reports, allen thinks that today’s retirees are less willing to sacrifice their lifestyles. Reverse mortgage proceeds can fund a variety of uses — from family vacations to in-home care that eases the load on adult children, or even a move into a 55-plus community without draining savings.

According to recent reports, “That’s why I love this business, because it’s infinitely customizable,” he mentioned. “Every client is unique, every situation is unique, and we have this expanding suite of products to really help deliver for the clients … so that they can get the joy out of the transaction.”.

New research highlights how runtime protection, AI security and managed services are transforming cloud security, creating significant opportunities for technology providers and enterprises.

LONDON, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The global cloud security market is poised for transformational growth, with revenues projected to increase from $8.4 billion in 2025 to $26.8 billion by 2031, representing a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 21.4%, according to new research from Frost & Sullivan.

The manufacturer's latest analysis, Total Cloud Security Market, Global, 2025â2031, reveals how the convergence of cloud-native technologies, AI-driven workloads and increasingly sophisticated cyber threats is accelerating demand for integrated security platforms capable of protecting complex hybrid and multi-cloud environments.

As enterprises move beyond traditional cloud security tools focused on visibility, configuration management and vulnerability detection, attention is shifting towards extended cloud security (XCS) platforms that unify protection across applications, infrastructure, workloads, identities, data and AI systems.

Frost & Sullivan identifies three particularly promising areas for commercial development.

Industry observers note that runtime-informed cloud security operations are gaining momentum as enterprises seek to move beyond identifying vulnerabilities towards understanding which threats pose genuine risks in production environments. This is driving demand for solutions that combine real-time threat detection, exploitability analysis, contextual risk prioritisation and coordinated remediation.

Meanwhile, the proliferation of generative AI applications, autonomous agents and AI-powered workloads is expanding the cloud attack surface, creating opportunities for AI security capabilities that integrate model protection, sensitive data security, identity governance and AI runtime monitoring into existing cloud security platforms.

According to recent reports, growing operational complexity and shortages of specialist cybersecurity talent are also fuelling demand for managed cloud security services. Managed security providers, systems integrators and cloud partners are increasingly positioned to help enterprises implement integrated security architectures, manage continuous monitoring and translate security findings into actionable risk reduction.

Anh Tien Vu, Industry Principal, Global Cybersecurity, Frost & Sullivan, commented:.

It has been revealed that "The cloud security market is moving beyond visibility, posture, and fragmented control toward the unified extended cloud security platform model that connects code, cloud, runtime, data, identity, AI, and SOC workflows. The next phase of growth will be defined by platforms that do not simply find risk, but validate and prioritize it, assign ownership, accelerate remediation, and support real-time threat detection and response across complex hybrid and multi-cloud environments.".

While North America is expected to remain the largest regional market, expanding cloud adoption, regulatory pressures and demand for managed security capabilities will continue to generate opportunities across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America.

As cloud environments become increasingly interconnected and AI-driven, Frost & Sullivan expects competitive differentiation to depend less on the volume of threats identified and more on the ability to translate security intelligence into measurable risk reduction and operational resilience.

In a recent development, nvidia, IBM and Fermilab confirmed newly introduced tools for quantum error correction on Nov. 16, and the news comes amid a debate in the crypto industry about "Q-Day," the moment when a quantum computer will be able to break Bitcoin's cryptography. As of Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $64,580.

In a recent development, nvidia released a newly introduced decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, on Nov. 16. According to the tech giant, the algorithm delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms, and it cuts the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to 45 minutes.

Nvidia remarked that the algorithm helps researchers find designs that use physical qubits more efficiently, "shortening the path to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.".

According to recent reports, nvidia and IBM also declared plans for a modular quantum computing codesign platform with Fermilab. IBM and Nvidia are placing Nvidia DGX B200 systems next to IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, and researchers will use the platform to develop and test error-correction codes.

"Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together," said Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at Nvidia.

A 2022 study by researchers from the University of Sussex estimated that breaking Bitcoin's encryption within a day would require around 13 million physical qubits.

IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM calls its fastest quantum processor, has 120 qubits. According to Nvidia, errors in quantum processors "limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform.".

In a recent development, in 2024, Bitcoin developer Hunter Beast proposed BIP-360, a new output type that would protect coins from quantum attacks. In July 2025, Casa co-founder Jameson Lopp also suggested a proposal to phase out legacy signatures and move coins to quantum-resistant addresses.

Early coins mined by Satoshi Nakamoto sit on addresses with public keys that are already visible on the blockchain.

In November 2024, NIST proposed to stop allowing vulnerable public-key algorithms, including elliptic curve cryptography, after 2035.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 13:39 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Recent findings suggest that enterprises pushing AI from pilot to production are learning that data, not GPUs, is the hardest part, and open table formats such as Apache Iceberg are part of the answer. Demand for AI infrastructure indicates few signs of slowing, but much of the information companies need is still scattered, ungoverned and out of reach.

Industry observers note that that pressure is turning storage into an active layer that classifies, governs and serves data to models. Unstructured files such as logs and medical images hold intelligence AI can now extract, according to Arun Prasad Raman (pictured, left), vice president of hybrid cloud and AI infrastructure at Hitachi Vantara Corp.

Industry observers note that “Storage is not seen as just storing the data,” Raman said. “You need to bring in more intelligence natively rather than moving the data to another replication and bringing it back for, say, indexing. If it can do it natively, that’s where the value add is.”.

Recent findings suggest that raman and Jeff Lundberg (right), principal product and solutions manager at Hitachi Vantara, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI’s pilot-to-production gap, Apache Iceberg and how Hitachi Vantara is adding intelligence to storage. (* Disclosure below.).

Industry observers note that reference architectures for AI factories and data platforms are largely settled. Most projects stall because data is spread across on-premises systems, software-as-a-service applications and the cloud, while access control, governance and shifting regulations add friction, according to Lundberg. Hitachi Vantara is responding with industry-specific solutions built on its Hitachi iQ stack and its sister businesses’ rail and energy experience, he explained.

It has been revealed that “It’s about the outcome more so than the technology that we’re trying to put into place,” Lundberg mentioned. “That’s an enabler to get you to the solution you’re trying to get to.”.

Sources indicate that much of that work now happens in storage. Last week, Hitachi Vantara expanded its VSP One platform with new object storage and data lakehouse capabilities. A service in its object store flags files containing personal information, such as Social Security numbers. Data scientists can then keep that data out of specific models or block its replication to another country, Raman explained.

“That’s the intelligence we are adding into the storage itself,” Raman stated. “So that’s where the evolution of storage is making it more intelligent.”.

Analytics follow the same logic. CT scan metadata can be stored in Apache Iceberg format on the manufacturer’s object store and queried directly. An application could list every abdominal scan from the past year without a separate extract, transform and load or ETL process or database, Raman noted.

Sources indicate that “Whether it’s a backup or it’s 10 years old, it still carries some intelligence,” Raman said. “As long as it carries intelligence, it becomes important to AI.”.

  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm.
  • A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S.
  • In a recent development, the research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm.

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

In a recent development, the research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

According to recent reports, guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”.

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

Sources indicate that in the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

According to recent reports, the study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

All three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for new clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

In a recent development, “So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elite university Harvard maintains significant Bitcoin exposure as it holds over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin ETF, a recent regulatory filing has revealed.

Harvard University remains highly exposed to Bitcoin (BTC) as the elite institution continues to hold over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF).

Industry observers note that as per Bitcoin Magazine’s Nov. 16 report, Harvard Management Firm, which manages Harvard University’s endowment, held 3,044,612 shares of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

According to recent reports, the Form 13F filing by Harvard University with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) showed that its investment in the Bitcoin ETF was worth roughly $144.1 million at the end of the third quarter.

Notably, Harvard did not change its Bitcoin ETF share count during the third quarter. The university held the same number of shares as reported at the end of June.

Harvard first disclosed its investment in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF during the second quarter of 2025.

As per Harvard's Form 13F filing submitted on Aug. 8, 2025, it held 1,906,000 IBIT shares at the end of the second quarter. The investment was worth roughly $116.7 million as of June 30.

The university subsequently increased its Bitcoin exposure significantly.

For instance, at the end of September 2025, Harvard held 6,813,612 IBIT shares, worth roughly $442.9 million. The Bitcoin ETF was the biggest investment that Harvard publicly reported at the time.

Later, however, the university started trimming its Bitcoin exposure. For example, during the fourth quarter of 2025, Harvard reduced its IBIT holdings by about 21.4%. Its total share holdings fell to 5.35 million.

During the first quarter of 2026, Harvard again reduced its Bitcoin exposure by 43.1%. This brought down the number of IBIT shares to roughly 3.04 million.

Industry observers note that since then, the university has maintained this number of shares. Harvard's quarter-end share count has remained unchanged in recent quarters.

Harvard University is not the only top-tier American university that has gained exposure to the biggest cryptocurrency by market capitalization.

In October 2024, Emory University became the first U.S. university endowment to publicly disclose its holdings in a Bitcoin ETF.

It held roughly 2.7 million shares of Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust, worth over $15 million at the time.

Meanwhile, in May 2025, Brown University disclosed its holdings of 105,000 shares of BlackRock's IBIT, worth roughly $4.9 million as of March 31 of that year.

Later, Brown doubled its stake, bringing its holdings to 212,500 shares.

Meanwhile, Dartmouth College has also joined the list of universities with exposure to cryptocurrency ETFs.

Industry observers note that in its recent filing, Dartmouth College disclosed that it held 201,531 IBIT shares. The investment was worth roughly $9.5 million as of the end of September 2026.

#6547. Texas’ population boom is opening doors for new real estate agents

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1007 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Texas’ population boom is opening doors for new real estate agents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few states are changing as rapidly as Texas.
  • Texas’ population has passed 31 million, and the suburbs surrounding Dallas, Houston, Austin and San Antonio are stretching farther and farther out.
  • Expensive markets with little buildable land work differently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few states are changing as rapidly as Texas. It added more people than any other state between 2024 and 2025, and builders there got the green light for more new homes in 2025 than anywhere else in the country. More people and more houses mean more deals to be done, and more room for new agents to get in on them.

Texas’ population has passed 31 million, and the suburbs surrounding Dallas, Houston, Austin and San Antonio are stretching farther and farther out. Competition has cooled compared with the pandemic boom, yet the demand behind the market continues to climb.

Expensive markets with little buildable land work differently. In Texas, the business depends on sheer size, people relocating and a pipeline of newly built homes.

Recent findings suggest that over the 12 months ending July 2025, Texas grew by 391,243 people, a bigger gain than any other state posted. The population now sits near 31.7 million, 8.8% higher than in 2020.

It has been revealed that each newcomer is a future tenant, homebuyer or seller, and many will start households of their own. That means agents don’t have to count on climbing prices for opportunity. The bigger driver is people relocating and settling in for the long haul.

Recent findings suggest that raw population counts miss how often Texans relocate. In 2024, the state accounted for 7.8% of every move between states, a share topped only by Florida. Meanwhile, 3.4 million residents changed addresses without leaving Texas, the highest in-state figure in the nation.

More newcomers still come from California than from anywhere else. Once all the arrivals and departures between states are netted out, Texas came out roughly 73,000 residents ahead.

According to recent reports, all that activity is what keeps agents busy. A client arriving from out of state and one moving a few miles away both need help, which gives relocation-focused agents a reliable stream of business in and around the significant metros.

Look at every U.S. city with 20,000 or more residents, and the five growing fastest are all in Texas. Fulshear, outside Houston, is the only one that isn’t in the Dallas-Fort Worth orbit.

It has been revealed that austin hit 1 million residents that same year, becoming the fifth Texas city of that size alongside Houston, San Antonio, Dallas and Fort Worth. For new real estate agents, though, the bigger openings are in suburbs, master-planned developments and up-and-coming markets, not city centers.

No state approved permits for more newly introduced homes in 2025 than Texas, which authorized 210,217 units. Dallas and Houston ranked first and second among all U.S. metros, with Austin seventh.

All three metros issued fewer permits than in 2024, yet each is still well ahead of most of the nation. Whole subdivisions are under construction right now, and that work supports agents who sell fresh builds, partner with builders, focus on master-planned communities, help relocating families or guide people buying their first home.

Statewide active listings were up 2.8% in Q3 2026, and 18 of Texas’ 26 metros saw inventory increase. The median price across the state dipped 0.4% to $333,628, even as 15 metros posted price gains and 12 recorded more sales.

That extra selection lets buyers shop around. Sellers, meanwhile, are counting on their agents to set a smart price, present the home well, get it seen and negotiate effectively.

Among Texas REALTORS® surveyed in 2026, 69% said their buyers faced no competing offers, compared with 57% a year earlier. Seventy-one percent described buyers’ search timelines as ample or reasonable, and only 6% blamed a stalled search on thin inventory.

That changes what clients need from an agent. Outbidding the competition matters less than helping buyers choose well. The agents who stand out have deep neighborhood knowledge, can lay out what different homes will really cost each month and know how to get the most out of builder incentives.

Being a trusted advisor counts for more than processing forms.

International purchasers bought roughly 7,780 Texas homes from April 2025 through March 2026, spending a combined $4 billion. Texas captured 12% of the nation’s international homebuyers over that stretch.

Industry observers note that buyers from Mexico made up the biggest group, with India, China, Nigeria and the U.K. rounding out the top five. More than half, 58%, settled in the suburbs. Agents comfortable with overseas relocations and cross-border transactions have an expanding specialty to tap into, and much of it is in suburban markets.

Texas leaves plenty of room to shape your own business. One agent might become the go-to expert in a single booming suburb. Another might focus on new construction where builders are most active, or on families arriving from out of state or relocating within Texas.

Other specialties are open too, from international clients to first-time buyers, move-up buyers and rental investors. You also get to decide whether you’d rather work in a large metro or one of the state’s smaller fast-growing towns.

Industry observers note that whichever direction you choose, expect paychecks to be inconsistent at first. Every specialty depends on regular lead generation and on building relationships over time.

In a recent development, texas requires aspiring agents to finish 180 hours of qualifying education before they can be licensed. Colibri Real Estate delivers those courses online, so you can fit your studies around the job you already have.

If you choose a package with exam prep, you’ll also get practice exams and live sessions where instructors answer your questions, all aimed at getting you ready to pass.

Recent findings suggest that building a real estate career in Texas takes effort, and your first years will be spent generating leads and growing your business. Still, if you’re ready to do that work, the conditions are strong: millions of residents relocating, suburbs springing up and homebuilding happening on a massive scale.

It has been revealed that fresh households and new housing markets keep appearing across Texas. For agents committed to the work, there’s plenty of room to grow alongside them.

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

In a recent development, noeri’s software studies a company’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company stated.

Sources indicate that it works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the company noted.

Recent findings suggest that the pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin stated at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”.

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Industry observers note that guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Recent findings suggest that choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that taylor Swift, classical or silence?
  • In a recent development, ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

In a recent development, ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

Recent findings suggest that none could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He remarked he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

Sources indicate that “Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be stated for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Sources indicate that megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

It has been revealed that “I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan stated. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Sources indicate that jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

According to recent reports, “Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Industry observers note that agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Recent findings suggest that sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she remarked, but it highlighted cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova noted. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

Recent findings suggest that for mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and latest construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova mentioned. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney noted.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

According to recent reports, he also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

According to recent reports, “In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer noted. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

According to recent reports, she played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

It has been revealed that shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea states she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

Recent findings suggest that marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, Newly introduced Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

Recent findings suggest that his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

According to recent reports, “Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he stated. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

It has been revealed that on setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Sources indicate that bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Industry observers note that kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she mentioned.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova noted she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

According to recent reports, so the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has shared the reason the XRP Ledger (XRPL) used code and cryptography from Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, in its early stages.

In his Nov. 16 post on X, Schwartz said they primarily chose to do so for security reasons and to prevent backlash from the Bitcoin community when the XRP Ledger was still in its early development.

The conversation started when prominent XRPL validator Vet (@Vet_X0) pointed out how some of Satoshi Nakamoto's initial design decisions are still present in the XRP Ledger's structure.

Vet noted that the XRP Ledger initially used helper functions from the original Bitcoin software, including timekeeping functions coded by Satoshi Nakamoto himself.

Industry observers note that some of those helper functions were reportedly copied by Jed McCaleb, one of the early developers of the XRP Ledger. The original Bitcoin code even included a comment left by the mysterious creator of Bitcoin.

Afterward, Schwartz shared the reason why XRP Ledger developers opted to use the cryptographic options from Bitcoin instead of creating upcoming ones.

"We did things that way in the very early days because we didn't want to be potentially facing criticism that our choices for those core crypto functions were less secure than Bitcoin's," stated Schwartz.

In other words, XRP Ledger developers opted to use Bitcoin's cryptographic options to avoid possible controversial security-related decisions when creating a new cryptocurrency network.

Later on, Vet asked Schwartz if their decision helped gain acceptance among Bitcoin supporters who looked at their protocol in its early stages.

Schwartz mentioned it was hard to say whether it helped or not.

"It's hard to say. Obviously we never got those criticisms. But it's hard to know if we would have," Schwartz mentioned.

Additionally, the Ripple executive pointed out that it was uncertain whether the developers could have come up with better options if they had chosen to make their own cryptographic decisions.

"I'm not sure we would have come up with better ones had we made our own decisions anyway," Schwartz wrote.

It is worth noting that the original Bitcoin code copied in the early stages of the XRP Ledger is no longer present in the network's codebase.

According to Vet, the remaining parts of Satoshi Nakamoto's timekeeping code were deleted in December 2014 by former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis.

There are two crucial cryptographic design decisions from Bitcoin that are still used on the XRP Ledger.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:21 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Sources indicate that as artificial intelligence workloads shift to inference, memory bandwidth decides whether hardware generates tokens swiftly or sits idle. D-Matrix Corp. is answering with Raptor, a second-generation chip stacking 3D DRAM beneath its compute logic.

AI infrastructure has become a systems game, and winners combine memory, interconnect and software into cohesive designs, according to Satyam Srivastava (pictured), fellow at d-Matrix.

It has been revealed that “It’s no longer a chip problem. Chip plays a part of it. Memory bandwidth is a fundamental advantage that has to be solved,” Srivastava stated. “The next is energy efficiency. The next is interconnect efficiency. The next is software cohesiveness.”.

It has been revealed that srivastava spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed d-Matrix’s Raptor chip and its stacked 3D DRAM, inference memory bandwidth and the shift toward heterogeneous computing. (* Disclosure below.).

D-Matrix proves each risky technology on a test chip first. Jayhawk proved die-to-die connectivity, and Jayhawk II validated digital in-memory computing. The Corsair accelerator combined both and entered full production earlier this year, Srivastava explained.

“Fast forward, we have the Pavehawk chip, test chip, which is proving out 3D DRAM stacked underneath the logic die, which serves as the core technology for Raptor, which is our second-generation chip coming out next year,” Srivastava said.

Stacking keeps the distributed memory architecture intact but moves memory cells onto a separate layer rather than consuming logic die area. Data travels a short distance and never crosses an interposer. That puts 3D DRAM in a new tier between SRAM and high-bandwidth memory, Srivastava noted.

“So you’re getting 10 times higher energy efficiency compared to HBM, 10 times higher bandwidth compared to HBM, where it sits in between SRAM and HBM in terms of capacity,” Srivastava mentioned.

Pairing a Corsair-based server with an existing Hopper GPU fleet can raise utilization from about 20% to as much as 80%, meaning more tokens per dollar, Srivastava noted. D-Matrix has also adopted NVLink Fusion rackscale infrastructure from Nvidia Corp. to connect its accelerators to Nvidia’s AI factories.

“For us, it unlocks the opportunity to participate in a very established ecosystem, the world’s most popular AI factory. We get access to a very hardened design of an MGX rack,” Srivastava noted.

The partnership points toward heterogeneous computing, where software orchestrates GPUs, CPUs and accelerators such as Raptor as one system, with the cluster as the unit of computing, Srivastava explained.

In a recent development, “So think of a chip, but that chip is an entire cluster and it has many different hardware units,” Srivastava stated. “Some are GPUs, some are CPUs, some are ASIC accelerators, and you can use whichever one you like to serve the needs of the workload the best.”.
