  • 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AlphaPoint, a provider of institutional digital asset infrastructure since 2013, today introduced the Approval Device, a dedicated hardware device with its own secure display and an optional FIPS 140-3-certified secure element, designed to help businesses protect their most sensitive actions in an increasingly hostile, AI-driven threat environment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dedicated hardware lets authorized employees review and approve sensitive requests separately from their computers, adding an independent checkpoint as attacks become harder to spot.

FRESH YORK, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AlphaPoint, a provider of institutional digital asset infrastructure since 2013, today introduced the Approval Device, a dedicated hardware device with its own secure display and an optional FIPS 140-3-certified secure element, designed to help businesses protect their most sensitive actions in an increasingly hostile, AI-driven threat environment.

Designed to integrate with existing systems, the Approval Device adds a hacker-resistant approval step to the workflows that matter most, such as administrative changes, payments and access to sensitive data. AI hacking makes laptops, workstations and mobile phones vulnerable, and the Approval Device helps protect administrative and security-critical workflows. Its software is written using security-first best practices and formally verified programming languages for safety and correctness, and it uses no complex operating system such as Linux, Windows or macOS, keeping its attack surface to an absolute minimum.

It has been revealed that even if an attacker has taken over an employee's other work devices, the Approval Device clearly highlights the action about to be processed. Hardware wallets protect cryptocurrency transactions the same way, and the Approval Device brings that model to traditional business workflows beyond the blockchain.

According to recent reports, an easy-to-use SDK lets human and AI programmers connect the device to the processes that matter most to your business. Once connected, it protects them from employee system compromise.

AlphaPoint is providing an evaluation kit to businesses, please contact us for more information.

Employee systems can perform consequential actions through business administration software, websites, and mobile applications. Multi-party approval flows offer enhanced security and continuity. During onboarding, humans and AI systems help identify what needs protection and who can approve those actions.

Sources indicate that when one of those actions is requested, the designated approvers review it on the device's own screen and deliberately hold to approve or decline. A compromised computer can show one request while submitting another, but the device indicates only the real one, and each approval is cryptographically bound to that exact request. Policy controls then confirm every required approval is in place before the action goes ahead.

"Attackers keep winning with the same classes of vulnerabilities. They rarely need anything fresh, because the old weaknesses keep working. We decided to stop fighting them one patch at a time. The Approval Device is designed to take entire classes of attack off the table, not just the latest example of each. That means a far smaller attack surface, far fewer ways in, and employee systems that are far harder to compromise," remarked Joe Ventura, CTO of AlphaPoint.

Potential applications include changes to administrative permissions, updates to critical system settings, releases of sensitive information and transfers of funds. Organizations can define approval requirements around the consequences of an action, including additional approvers for higher-risk requests.

The Approval Device works with Secure Core, which is designed to keep sensitive business logic, data and credentials separate from everyday application systems, protect keys in hardware, and keep signed, exportable records of every approval.

Industry observers note that alphaPoint works as a design partner to identify the workflows an organization needs to protect, define approval policies and support integration and validation within its existing systems. A 30-minute security briefing under NDA provides an opportunity to review the architecture, threat model and verification evidence.

Sources indicate that to arrange a call, visit alphapoint.com/alphapoint-cloud. Qualified companies receive a free evaluation kit containing physical equipment for evaluation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm.

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the company announced Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

It has been revealed that fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

Guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the company said. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the tech giant says other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

Sources indicate that “At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon stated in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”.

It has been revealed that breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The company went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

#6539. Industry News: Which way is down, revisited

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (740 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Which way is down, revisited

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2008, HousingWire published an analysis asking whether severe mortgage delinquencies were pushing home prices down, or falling prices were pushing delinquencies up.
  • Seventeen of 20 major metros highlighted a significant negative correlation between 60-plus-day delinquencies and Case-Shiller prices.
  • The 2026 market looks very different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2008, HousingWire published an analysis asking whether severe mortgage delinquencies were pushing home prices down, or falling prices were pushing delinquencies up.

Seventeen of 20 major metros highlighted a significant negative correlation between 60-plus-day delinquencies and Case-Shiller prices. Granger causality tests found delinquency trends and predicted price trends in 13 metros; six showed a two-way relationship, and only San Francisco showed prices leading delinquencies. In most markets, distress appeared to be part of the mechanism driving prices lower.

The 2026 market looks very different. Delinquencies are rising year over year while nominal prices still rise nationally. The 2008 relationship may not have vanished, but the housing-credit system may have moved into a different causal regime.

The Mortgage Bankers Association reported a 4.37% national delinquency rate in the second quarter, 44 basis points above a year earlier. The 90-day rate edged up to 1.43%, foreclosures stood at 0.67% of loans and the seriously delinquent rate rose for a fourth straight quarter.

It has been revealed that yet the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller National Index rose 1.9% year over year in July, the 20-City Composite 2.5% and FHFA’s index 2.6%. Prices have fallen in real terms for 14 straight months, though much of July’s 3.4% inflation was energy-driven; core inflation was 2.5%. The market combines nominal stability, real erosion and rising credit stress, a configuration unlike 2008.

Recent findings suggest that conventional delinquency was 2.72%, VA 4.89% and FHA 11.79%, with FHA up 122 basis points in a year. ATTOM counted 40,277 foreclosure filings in August, up 13%, with completed foreclosures up 42%. Activity remains far below the 2008–2010 crisis, which helps explain why rising delinquency has not collapsed prices.

It has been revealed that equity is also uneven. ATTOM found 3.2% of mortgaged homes seriously underwater in the second quarter, up from 2.7% a year earlier. Minnesota led at 12.1%, up from 2.6%, while second-ranked Louisiana, at 10.3%, improved from 11.9%. Underwater share measures vulnerability, not distress itself.

Industry observers note that chicago led the Case-Shiller metros in July at 6.9%; Seattle (−1.6), Las Vegas (−1.3) and Denver (−1.1) declined. That 8.5-point spread reflects different regimes within one national economy. A market can carry distress without falling prices if supply is tight, and a falling market can breed delinquency if equity is thin. The relevant unit is the local borrower-market system, not the nation.

It has been revealed that the 2008 mechanism was distressed supply: delinquency, foreclosures and REO, lower prices, lower equity, more delinquency. It remains valid, but today’s distressed pipeline is far smaller, so the default-to-price channel may be weaker in aggregate. The reverse channel, in which lower prices erode equity and raise default incentives for leveraged borrowers, may matter more.

The better question is no longer which comes first, but under what conditions the direction changes. One hypothesis: in a normal regime the link is weak; in an equity-stress regime falling prices drive delinquency; in a distressed-supply regime concentrated delinquency drives prices; in a feedback regime both operate at once. That is a framework to test, not a finding.

Whether the 2008 relationship holds today is untested; I am not aware of a published re-estimation across the post-crisis period.

A modern version should use metro-level price and delinquency series from roughly 2000 to 2026, retain the Granger framework for comparability, test for cointegration, add controls for unemployment, mortgage rates, loan type, leverage and equity, and test whether coefficients shift once thresholds such as cumulative price declines, negative equity or serious delinquency are crossed.

This article does not replicate the original tests, which used proprietary loan-level data; comparable public metro delinquency series are not available in the same form.

In 2008, delinquency, foreclosure and falling prices reinforced one another nationally. In 2026, credit stress is rising while nominal prices hold and metros diverge. The evidence suggests the relationship may have changed; it does not yet show how. Which channel dominates may depend on the state of the market. The question may be less which way is down than when the direction changes, and risk models should treat causality as a function of the regime.

Sources indicate that source: Showalter and Cho, HousingWire, Nov./Dec. 2008. Data as of Oct. 5, 2026.

Young Cho, Ph.D., is the Founder and CEO of PalmBridge Investment.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

Axelera AI B.V. built its business at the edge with low-power chips and edge AI development tools, and it is now taking that technology into data center infrastructure, according to Manuel Botija (pictured), vice president and head of product at Axelera.

“Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure. They’re locked out because of the cost and the power,” Botija noted. “We are enabling them now to own it. Industry observers note that “Now you can own your own infrastructure,” Botija remarked. “You can amortize those investments and … reduce your opex, and therefore be more profitable as a tech giant.”.

Most Local Businesses in West Virginia Can Expect Measurable SEO Improvements Within Three to Six Months of Consistent Effort.

Industry observers note that CHARLESTON, W. Va., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- How long does it realistically take for a local business in West Virginia to see results from search engine optimization? A HelloNation article addresses this question with a practical look at SEO timelines, explaining the variables that shape how quickly local business SEO efforts begin to show measurable returns.

Recent findings suggest that the article explains that for most businesses in the state, measurable improvements tend to appear within three to six months of consistent work. That range is intentionally wide. It reflects the number of variables involved, including where the website starts, how competitive the market is, and the quality of the optimization effort itself.

Recent findings suggest that where a business begins matters significantly. A organization that has never invested in SEO starts with little to no domain authority, minimal indexed content, and no established backlink profile. A business with an existing website has a foundation to build from, even if it has been neglected for some time. The gap between those two situations directly affects how quickly early progress becomes visible.

Sources indicate that competition shapes the timeline as well. In smaller West Virginia markets, a business offering a niche service in a specific county may see local business SEO results more promptly than a business chasing broad terms in a larger metro area. The article notes that targeting well-defined, locally specific keywords consistently outperforms trying to rank for national or highly competitive terms in the early stages of a campaign.

Website quality is another factor. Search engines evaluate how fast a site loads, how well it functions on mobile devices, and how easy it is to crawl and index. A site with significant technical problems may see slower progress even when other optimization work is being done well.

It has been revealed that digital Marketing Expert Sean O'Kelly's insights, as featured in the article, make clear that the early months of a local business SEO campaign in West Virginia require patience. Initial results are often incremental. A business might begin appearing in results for terms where it previously had no presence at all, or see rankings move from a deeper page toward the first. This early progress is meaningful, even if it does not immediately translate into more calls or form submissions.

It has been revealed that traffic growth generally follows ranking improvements by several weeks. As rankings stabilize in stronger positions, more customers see and click the result. As more users visit and engage with the site, those behavioral signals reinforce the ranking further. The process compounds over time, which is one reason consistency matters so much throughout the early stages.

Recent findings suggest that businesses that pause local business SEO efforts during the first few months often find they are restarting the clock when they resume. Search engines respond to sustained signals of relevance and credibility. Inconsistent effort tends to produce inconsistent results. By the six-to-twelve-month mark, a business that has stayed committed to on-page optimization, local citation building, content creation, and technical maintenance typically sees meaningful traffic growth and a measurable increase in leads from organic search. For most markets in West Virginia, the competitive landscape is manageable enough that a well-executed strategy can build a clear advantage within a year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:11 am.

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it plans to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey said he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems.

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

According to recent reports, humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

“Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey mentioned today in a news release. “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”.

Ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

In a recent development, carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The company says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

Artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey stated. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”.

Recent findings suggest that greg Scofield, an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, noted Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034.

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

Sources indicate that radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small firm.

Humphrey stated the company right now has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. Back in 2022, Radian announced a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

According to recent reports, so, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey noted. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”.

He acknowledged that following through on the plan for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he mentioned.

Humphrey said the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the company’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he said. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”.

Is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace firm? Humphrey noted that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he said. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. It’s just the way I’ve come to accept it.”.

Breaking: The power of agile workflows

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every leader in this industry knows that every dollar matters, every teammate matters and every borrower matters.
  • Agile workflows aren’t made of “unicorns and rainbows” and “all things possible” energy, but they are the answer to this.
  • In a recent development, our industry’s cost of origination is at one of the highest points in history ($10,936 per loan as of Q2 2026).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every leader in this industry knows that every dollar matters, every teammate matters and every borrower matters. However, when we try to prioritize all of these, something often has to give. What if we didn’t have to compromise, though? What if it were possible to reduce costs, optimize your team and create a fast, easy borrower experience?

Agile workflows aren’t made of “unicorns and rainbows” and “all things possible” energy, but they are the answer to this.

In a recent development, our industry’s cost of origination is at one of the highest points in history ($10,936 per loan as of Q2 2026). When approximately 70% of that cost is our operating overhead, how effective and efficient our teams are REALLY matters.

In a recent development, today, most of our industry’s teams and technology operate around an extremely linear process that requires our borrowers to fit into our process that was designed to move paper. So, the borrowers that give you 100% of what you need on day one have the same process as the borrower who drags their feet and gets you what you need piece by piece.

We might be able to get one cleared to close a bit faster than the other, but both borrowers went from their loan officer to their processor, to an underwriter, back to a processor, back to the underwriter, then to closing. Every single one of those handoffs adds time, costs and frustration to the borrower who just wants to know if they are approved promptly and if they can close on time.

It has been revealed that agile workflows queue work to be completed when the data and documents say that the work can be completed. They don’t rely on milestones or handoffs.

For example, if a borrower has all of their income and employment documentation and data submitted but they haven’t found a property yet, that loan’s income and employment can still be queued for review by a decision maker (technology or an underwriter…it’s up to your organization’s risk threshold) who can issue that borrower’s income/employment approval, NOT pre-approval. We don’t have to wait until they find a property or until they go through processing.

According to recent reports, queuing work this way gives certainty to borrowers with a faster feedback loop. So, that borrower who brings everything in on day one finally gets rewarded for it. It also ensures that your team is only working on what matters most. They have work queued to them when it’s needed and the rest of their time can be spent building relationships with borrowers and referral partners.

That’s the borrower and team side. Now, let’s talk about cost. Every loan we originate has to meet very specific criteria from the GSEs or from private investors. So we can’t necessarily eliminate work that has to be completed, but we can eliminate handoffs, assign work to technology solutions, and reduce rework.

Let’s start here: Have you ever measured your cost per file touch? It’s your fulfillment cost divided by the total number of touches across your files. If you really want to dig into this even further, you can measure this by role type to see the cost of how many times your underwriter vs your closer vs your processor vs your AI agent touches the file.

I’m not suggesting we eliminate roles reviewing things when it’s needed, but I am saying that unnecessary reviews do cost an organization more than most of us realize.

According to recent reports, reducing unnecessary touches is critical, but that’s not really the power of agile workflows. Agile workflows are the answer because they queue the right touches exactly when they’re needed to the exact right person on your team or the exact right technology that can complete the work on your behalf. It’s orchestrating the work between your team and your technology in a way that reduces friction while controlling risk.

This isn’t easy to operationalize, though. It requires three major shifts: building your workflow around data triggers instead of milestones, assigning decision authority by risk threshold of the work and measuring cost per file touch. Then, you have to align your team’s roles, expectations and incentive plans around these shifts.

This is A LOT, but it is possible with almost every LOS provider out there (including the one you’re likely already on), and the rewards are incredible for your team, your borrowers and your company.

I know we’ve been told that we have to choose between efficient teams, happy borrowers and our bottom line, but there is a better way. Agile workflows are the answer.

Tech Report: NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO notes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • In a recent development, pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

In a recent development, pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO remarked he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint remarked he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

White also allegedly stated that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or blueprint.”.

According to recent reports, pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

Recent findings suggest that “NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

In a recent development, pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears stated the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

Recent findings suggest that “John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

In a recent development, “Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.
  • According to recent reports, revenue more than doubled year-over-year.
  • This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was revealed on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:32 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

Nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

According to recent reports, revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the company’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was revealed on Nov. 12. Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that the resignation followed the “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the firm’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” Hours after Huang publicly said he would be willing to return, Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and would not take questions about the circumstances or the board’s ongoing investigation.

Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer who is now also serving as interim CEO, set the tone in her first minute: “Our ambition will not change. Our passion for innovation will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change.”.

According to recent reports, after listening to the call, I believe Nvidia answered the short-term question and left the long-term one open. The tech giant made a convincing case that it can execute without its founder. It has yet to show who decides where it goes next. Here are five things we learned and what they mean for those who buy, budget for or operate artificial intelligence infrastructure.

In a recent development, the fear going into the call was disruption. The quarter closed before Huang’s exit, so the results can’t settle that. The guidance can, and it went up. Hyperscalers brought Vera Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell required. The roadmap is set through Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028, and Kress mentioned the supply agreements extend through the end of the decade.

According to recent reports, she explained that the past month has been “Business as usual.” Kress added, “We’ve engaged with our customers, suppliers and partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She also noted that TSMC leadership was at Nvidia’s offices this week.

It has been revealed that I have long held that Nvidia’s moat was never the silicon. It’s the accumulated layers of systems, software and supply chain built around it. The past week was the first real test of that view, and so far, it’s holding. A yearly product cadence this complex runs on thousands of engineers and a supply chain planned years in advance.

In a recent development, asked about talent retention, Kress acknowledged that “there are diverse opinions” among employees while insisting they are “committed to doing their life’s work” at Nvidia. The company’s talent can’t be overstated, and although Huang was the face of the company, the employees are what made it tick.

Earlier this week, Cisco Systems Inc. CEO Chuck Robbins appeared with Brian Sozzi. When asked whether he still trusts Nvidia, Robbins replied immediately, “Absolutely.” He added, “The industry’s bigger than one person. I don’t care how good you are. There are a lot of smart people. There are 42,000 people at Nvidia. So I’m not all that concerned.” Huang may have been the most visible Nvidia employee, but the company is full of smart, driven people. Leadership understands this, and I expect turnover to have minimal impact.

It has been revealed that employee retention is a top-of-mind issue for Nvidia executives. Business Insider reported this week that the organization held its first all-hands meeting after Huang. The article noted that Kress declared intends to accelerate pay raises and equity grants, Jones discussed the CEO search and Buck outlined the roadmap. It’s reasonable to believe that Huang’s departure was a shock to employees, but the business goes on, and I expect things to settle down in short order.

Industry observers note that for information technology buyers, nothing changes about what you’ve ordered or planned over the next 18 to 24 months. Don’t pause a deployment because of a leadership headline. The advice I gave in August still applies: Welcome Nvidia’s simplification and hedge the dependency.

Recent findings suggest that one of the more interesting comments on the call came from Jones, not Kress. In describing the CEO search, which will consider both internal and external candidates, he mentioned the board “appreciates that we’re living in a world where advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are driving major changes in our marketplace. Our new CEO will need to navigate those waters carefully.”.

Sources indicate that that was paired with immediate action. On the morning of earnings, the board created a standing national security and export control oversight committee of three directors that will retain outside experts. Kress disclosed that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China and noted that the U.S. Commerce Department issued new export controls this week, which the company “still has some time to study.”.

Huang was a product visionary who also served as the industry’s chief diplomat. The board is now signaling that fluency in Washington is a core requirement, on par with technical vision.

According to recent reports, for IT leaders at multinationals, export policy is now a deployment variable. The new Commerce rule is intended to block remote access to advanced chips via data centers in third countries, so the location of your capacity and who can access it are now compliance questions. Bring your compliance team into AI infrastructure planning early.

According to recent reports, with demand still far ahead of supply, who gets Nvidia systems matters more than what they cost. Kress laid out the criteria more clearly than I’ve heard before. First are land, power and shell, meaning whether a customer’s facility is ready to receive and use the gear in the quarter it ships. Second is capital. Third, for customers that aren’t investment-grade, is proof of off-take, or evidence that someone has committed to use the capacity.

“All are getting the same pricing,” Kress said. “That is super crucial for us, and we just need to assure that they are ready on their side in terms of being able to accept the compute.”.

According to recent reports, those same factors were incorporated into the guidance. Kress noted the outlook “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The reality is that the AI bottleneck has shifted from the chip to the building, the grid and the balance sheet. Nvidia is serving as the industry’s underwriter, determining who is ready.

In a recent development, the lesson for enterprise buyers is that readiness is the currency. If you want on-premises systems, secure power, cooling and funding before requesting allocation. If you can’t, buy capacity from a provider that has already cleared this hurdle. In my view, this also helps explain why sovereign AI is growing so quickly for Nvidia. Those projects often arrive with land and power already in place.

Sources indicate that over the past year, Nvidia has used its balance sheet to seed the ecosystem through guarantees, investments, and commitments to neoclouds and AI labs. Though  neoclouds remain vital, Kress brought a different tone to this audience. She mentioned Nvidia will “continue to be disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and that it is “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees” as other sources of capital become available. Asked about vendor financing, she acknowledged that “a lot of things have changed over this last quarter.”.

Industry observers note that two notable details emerged during the call. When Bernstein Research analyst Stacy Rasgon pressed on what he read as upcoming disclosure language about neocloud commitments, Kress explained that Nvidia’s guarantees take effect only after a partner has raised its own debt and equity, built the facility and installed the compute. If the project stalls, the guarantee lapses.

“Is it upcoming? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said. Even so, spelling it out clarifies Nvidia’s participation in neoclouds. When asked about uses of capital beyond the share buyback, which she said Nvidia still aims to complete, she put suppliers first: “The top priority is going to be our suppliers.” Prepayments to expand capacity come before customer financing, which will be reserved for “very strong customers.”.

Industry observers note that this was a critical piece of information for investors. I’ve previously compared vendor-financed neoclouds to the CLECs of the internet era, where the financing organization was left holding the bag. A CFO-led Nvidia appears to see the same risk. The result is a shakeout in which well-capitalized neoclouds with contracted demand grow stronger, while thinly funded ones struggle to secure systems. This should offer some comfort to investors that circular financing has been de-risked.

Recent findings suggest that the flip side is that someone still must fund the buildout outside the hyperscalers. Kress pointed to infrastructure capital partners establishing financing platforms. Whether that money arrives as fast as Nvidia steps back is what to watch for.

It has been revealed that my advice to IT buyers is to ask, before signing a multiyear deal with a neocloud, how it’s financed, how much capacity is committed and where it stands in Nvidia’s allocation queue. Those were niche questions a year ago. They should be standard due diligence now.

Industry observers note that the demand story has shifted from training models to running agents, broadening what customers need from Nvidia. Citing OpenRouter data, Kress mentioned agentic workloads now account for roughly 80% of tokens. Falling token prices are driving more usage, keeping GPU rental rates climbing.

It has been revealed that the CPU growth story shouldn’t surprise anyone. In May, I wrote that agentic AI opens a massive latest spigot for Nvidia on the CPU side. This quarter, demand outpaced supply. “Agentic AI is driving extraordinary demand for CPUs, far outstripping supply,” Kress remarked, noting that Nvidia’s Vera CPU is now adopted by CoreWeave, Meta, Nscale and Open AI. Agents spend much of their time calling tools, running code and moving data, which is general-purpose work. A CPU shortage amid a GPU boom shows how swiftly the workload is changing.

Nvidia is also filling in the layers above and around the hardware. The agent safety platform pairs OpenShell, which limits what agents can access, with Sentry, which runs on BlueField data processing units and monitors agent behavior in silicon. In my view, the biggest barrier to deploying agents in production is control, not model quality.

It has been revealed that the network is part of this, too. Kress said co-packaged optics is in volume production, and Lambda’s deployment, declared at this week’s SC26 conference, is the first large-scale proof point. Nvidia is a formidable networking vendor, though buyers mixing accelerators will still want to weigh a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing chip.

For IT buyers, strategy CPU capacity for agent workloads now, and insist that agent controls reside outside the model, in infrastructure you can audit.

Industry observers note that the question of who the newly introduced CEO will be might not be just about Nvidia but about the entire industry. If the board goes internal, Ian Buck seems to be the frontrunner. Externally, the names most bandied about are Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su, Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, or we could see Manuvir Das make a comeback and return to the company.

Most industry watchers describe Nvidia as a chip company, a view that is about a decade out of date. Nvidia’s value comes from the full systems it has built around its silicon. Each is a stack tailored to an industry: hardware, libraries, frameworks, pretrained models, simulation and developer tools, all tuned to work together.

In a recent development, the next CEO must treat silicon as a key layer of an open, secure, agentic enterprise stack. Enterprises won’t buy GPUs. They’ll buy outcomes: agents that run safely on governed data across clouds, on-premises and at the edge. Whoever runs Nvidia next must sell that outcome, play well within an ecosystem Nvidia doesn’t fully control, and make security a core part of the platform. Here are three dark-horse candidates to consider:.

Matt Garman. The Amazon Web Services Inc. CEO has led the world’s largest cloud through the shift to AI. He knows what it takes to turn infrastructure into consumable services at enormous scale. Garman also lives the open-stack approach: AWS offers model choice, runs its own Trainium chips alongside Nvidia’s, and sells to enterprises that want flexibility rather than lock-in. He would bring operational discipline and a deep feel for the customer. The question is whether Nvidia’s biggest customer-turned-competitor can credibly lead the supplier.

Industry observers note that jeetu Patel, Cisco Systems Inc.’s president and chief product officer, is the best storyteller in enterprise tech after Huang himself. He has spent the past few years rebuilding Cisco’s portfolio around secure AI infrastructure, integrating networking, security and observability into a single platform. That is exactly the “open, secure, agentic” stack Nvidia must deliver. Patel thinks in platforms, moves promptly,and has been personally using AI agents to shape his product views. He also has deep enterprise credibility, which Nvidia needs more than additional credibility with hyperscalers.

Charlie Giancarlo, CEO of Everpure (formerly Pure Storage), may be the most underrated name here. He built networking businesses at Cisco, spent time in private equity, and has repositioned Pure as a data management manufacturer. Storage revenue is growing thanks to hyperscaler wins. Giancarlo understands that agentic AI depends on data and that the data layer and the network are where enterprise AI succeeds or fails. He is a systems thinker who has led a platform transition before.

In a recent development, two final points on the CEO hire: For some reason, there is a tremendous amount of industry chatter that Jensen Huang was the only person at Nvidia with key relationships with suppliers, partners, and other ecosystem providers. I know for a fact that is not true. Nvidia’s leadership, which includes Buck, Deb Shoquist (executive vice president of operations), Nico Caprez (vice president of global AI development), Gilad Shainer and Kevin Deierling (networking leadership), Kress and others, all have deep relationships with the ecosystem.

In a recent development, also, I wouldn’t expect the board to make a snap decision about its next CEO. The roadmap is baked beyond Feynman, and the tech giant can continue for a couple of years, if needed. This is an important hire; the board should take its time and ensure it’s the right person.

This call confirmed what many industry watchers, including me, have long believed: The moat was built in layers, and those layers held. Supply is constrained, the roadmap is set and customers are still asking for more than Nvidia can build.

Kress closed the call by saying, “We’ve got this.” On execution, I believe her. Kress is a steady hand right now, and the discipline she brings to capital allocation should make the AI buildout healthier. The bets that created Nvidia’s position, though, were placed years before the market arrived. Post-Jensen, Nvidia will continue to perform as it did; as Robbins put it, no one is bigger than the industry.

My advice to IT buyers is to stick with current intends and closely monitor the CEO search. Since Nvidia’s roadmap is baked through Feynman and beyond, it can ride momentum for the next two years or longer.

  • Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup launched by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel prepares — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of users in its invite-only beta.
  • That includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am.

Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup launched by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel prepares — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of users in its invite-only beta.

That includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group. Vayo confirmed that its AI agents book there by navigating Expedia’s website, without a direct integration or partnership for those bookings.

The organization says Vayo recommends the best option for the traveler, wherever that option is booked, not just through its parent company’s brands.

Industry observers note that vayo is led by Mike Fridgen, a longtime Seattle entrepreneur with deep roots in travel. Booking Holdings, the parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, said last month that it plans to invest $100 million in Vayo, depending on its progress and market conditions.

Companies are still working out how to handle AI agents that use their sites on behalf of customers. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent didn’t identify itself.

According to recent reports, when Vayo rolled out last month, Fridgen remarked it was relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, in part to avoid the risk of being blocked. Vayo says no site has blocked its bookings so far.

Recent findings suggest that how the bookings work: Vayo’s newly introduced booking features work in two ways. It can book hotels, rental cars and activities through a direct connection with sister manufacturer Booking.com, and it has similar links to OpenTable for restaurants and SeatGeek for event tickets.

It has been revealed that for flights and other bookings, its AI agents navigate the booking websites, signing in to the traveler’s existing accounts where needed and completing the purchase. Every booking requires the traveler’s approval, the organization notes.

If a site doesn’t allow AI agents, Vayo leaves that booking to the traveler.

Sources indicate that vayo uses 1Password to sign in to travelers’ accounts and, on sites other than Booking.com, Stripe’s Link agent wallet to pay, without seeing their passwords or card details, the tech giant notes. It reports a reservation as confirmed only after the supplier confirms it.

Payments and pricing: Travelers pay whichever company they book with, and Vayo is not the merchant of record. The company declined to share details on commissions, saying its partner arrangements are still taking shape and won’t factor into its recommendations.

When Booking.com has the best option, Vayo customers get Genius Level 3 pricing, Booking.com’s top loyalty tier, with discounts of up to 20% on select stays.

It has been revealed that the service is free to use during the invite-only beta. Responding to GeekWire’s questions, Vayo didn’t say how many people are using it or how many have completed a booking.

Who’s behind Vayo: Fridgen, the Vayo co-founder and CEO, was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at airfare-prediction startup Farecast, before leading Decide.com and Madrona Venture Labs.

His co-founder and CTO is Allen Chen, the former CTO of Fanatics Collectibles, who previously co-founded Seattle software startups CloudPress and DataBlade. Ian Fliflet, OfferUp’s former chief growth officer, is head of growth. Vayo had about 20 employees, all working in downtown Seattle, when it launched last month.

Next on its product roadmap, the company says it plans to work inside the messaging apps people already use, and to let groups of travelers proposal trips together.

It has been revealed that HOUSTON, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ezee Fiber won two categories in the 2026 Fierce Network Innovation Awards, a leading telecommunications industry awards program. Its fiber-to-the-home expansion in Albuquerque and Santa Fe was named Broadband Build of the Year, and CEO Matt Marino was named Innovator of the Year.

The awards were confirmed and presented Nov. 19 during Broadband Nation Expo at the Hilton Riverside in Upcoming Orleans. The ceremony marked the first live, in-person presentation of the awards in the program's more than 15-year history.

Latest Mexico build recognized for measurable community impact.

The Broadband Build of the Year category honors completed builds with measurable community results. At the end of 2022, only about 4% of Bernalillo County and 9% of Santa Fe County could buy fiber at home. Ezee Fiber's $250 million New Mexico expansion, announced in 2023, now offers symmetrical residential speeds up to 8 Gbps and enterprise connectivity up to 400 Gbps, with no data caps.

A July 2026 Ezee Fiber-sponsored study by Dr. Brian Whitacre of Oklahoma State University ties roughly 661 local jobs to the rollout from 2021 to 2024 and estimates $77 million in home-value gains through 2025. More than 95% of the tech giant's Upcoming Mexico roles are filled locally, and it has invested $98 million in in-state supply chain spending.

After a 2025 stop-work order in Albuquerque, Ezee Fiber worked with city leaders on "neighbor-first" construction protocols that cut construction-related 311 calls by 47% year over year.

"This award belongs to our Upcoming Mexico team," said Pedro Checo, chief operating officer of Ezee Fiber. "New Mexico indicates what fiber can do when it's built with local people, local partners and a long-term commitment to the community.".

Marino named Innovator of the Year.

Since joining as CEO in 2023, Marino has built Ezee Fiber around the customer experience, pairing fast, reliable fiber with 24/7 local customer service. Under his leadership, that model is expanding from Texas and Fresh Mexico into Washington, Illinois, Oregon and Michigan.

In a recent development, "Together, these awards recognize the commitment of our teams to building better networks, delivering exceptional service and earning the trust of customers and communities," Marino noted. "Innovation is not simply about technology. It is about how effectively we deliver on our promises, solve problems and create lasting value for the people we serve.".

The recognition marks the inaugural presentation of Fierce Network's Innovator of the Year award and highlights the growing influence of emerging fiber providers in an industry historically dominated by much larger companies.

Hiring and recognition continue as the industry contracts.

According to recent reports, fierce Network honors add to a growing list of national industry recognitions for Ezee Fiber. PCMag named the company the best overall internet service provider in the U.S. for 2026 and included it among the Best Gaming ISPs (2025, 2026) and Fastest ISPs in the U.S. (2024, 2025).

Recent findings suggest that ezee Fiber has also earned 65 Speedtest by Ookla awards. A recent edition of Consumer Reports ranked Ezee Fiber among the nation's top 10 internet providers, with consumers praising its value, pricing and simplicity.

Recent findings suggest that the recognition comes as Ezee Fiber continues to expand its network, customer base and workforce across six states. While several major U.S. telecommunications companies have unveiled substantial workforce reductions, Ezee Fiber continues to invest in new markets and hire employees in sales, field operations, customer service and other functions. The company employs approximately 800 people and is targeting 200,000 customers and 800,000 homes passed by the end of 2026.

For more information about Ezee Fiber and service availability, visit www.ezeefiber.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After an important hackathon that demonstrated how AI agents could autonomously perform payments using blockchain, global payments giant Mastercard has spotlighted the XRP Ledger (XRPL).

36 hours. 179 hackers. 70 submissions. At the XRP Ledger Hackathon, developers used Mastercard Agent Pay for machines to explore upcoming possibilities for micropayments and autonomous commerce, including how AI agents can transact within defined spending limits and with verified merchants. See what we learned about the future of agentic commerce: https://t.co/S4NwQxxuRi #AgenticCommerce #DigitalAssets #AI.

Global payments giant Mastercard recently posted on X about the outcome of the XRP Ledger Hackathon. In the post, the payments firm detailed that 179 developers submitted 70 projects during the 36-hour event in Manhattan.

The focus of the competition was how to enable AI-powered agents to autonomously execute transactions and micropayments, engage with verified merchants and so forth, all while operating within budgets set by developers.

According to recent reports, the hackathon was held as part of the preparations for Ripple’s annual conference called Swell. Mastercard, Amazon Web Services, QuickNode and Ledger supported the event, which had a prize pool of over $40,000.

Mastercard published an official article in which it mentioned the challenge given to developers. They had to build AI agents that could autonomously make payments to verified merchants without human input.

Sources indicate that also, the agents had to operate within a specified budget. They had to settle payments using Ripple’s USD-backed stablecoin called RLUSD. They had to do this on the XRP Ledger.

One of the purposes of the challenge was to showcase how blockchain infrastructure can enable micropayments. This is especially the case for micropayments smaller than one cent.

In the future, these micropayments could be valuable as AI agents start buying computational resources or requesting data from other AI agents and then making payments themselves for digital services.

Mastercard’s vice president of digital assets, Michael Broderick, stressed that the organization's technology called Agent Pay for Machines could enable such payments.

Sources indicate that the project that won the competition is called Wraps. Its creators are Adarsha Mishra and Hrishabh Ayush. Their project dealt with how to secure user privacy in AI-based transactions. Their project demonstrated a method to prove that search logs were not being saved.

One of the most interesting things mentioned in the Mastercard report might be how the XRP Ledger is increasingly being used for payments by machines.

Mastercard mentioned that over 500,000 transactions are being conducted daily on the XRPL by AI agents.

Also, it’s reported that Ripple has recorded over 10 million payments using the x402 internet payment protocol on XRPL. This comes less than three months after the protocol crossed the 1 million payment milestone on the network.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am.

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a newly introduced CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no plans to change that.” He remarked he visits the company’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

It has been revealed that consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based firm acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Industry observers note that consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software tech giant Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and claims it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

According to recent reports, its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli mentioned Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

In a recent development, zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the company.

Sources indicate that zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but remarked Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by new pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

Zonar has added 1,000 new customers so far this year, a spokesperson said. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the manufacturer’s 2026 plan, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli stated.

Zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli said Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He said those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the big players.”.

Consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

“Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli noted. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”.

According to recent reports, founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The manufacturer cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

#6522. Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1999 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating upcoming requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure.
  • Agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure.
  • That shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:07 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Recent findings suggest that enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating upcoming requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure. While much of the early AI investment centered on access to powerful GPUs, organizations moving AI applications and agents into production are discovering that accelerators are only one part of the equation.

Agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure. That requires more than bare-metal GPU capacity. It calls for a complete cloud platform that combines compute, networking, storage, security and the services needed to manage applications at scale.

That shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them. Infrastructure providers increasingly need to support the full application lifecycle rather than simply supply specialized hardware.

During a live interview at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026, theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty spoke with Kevin Cochrane, chief marketing officer at Vultr, about the changing requirements of enterprise AI infrastructure, the return of CPU-based computing, data sovereignty and the growing role of platform engineering.

“They need a full cloud platform,” Cochrane said. “They need cloud compute, specialized AI compute, networking, storage and an open ecosystem.”.

In a recent development, vultr entered the cloud market in 2014 with a developer-focused platform built around performance, cost efficiency and accessibility. Since then, the tech giant has expanded into AI infrastructure, offering both traditional cloud services and specialized GPU resources.

Cochrane stated Vultr took a deliberate approach to the AI infrastructure market, prioritizing enterprise workload and platform-engineering requirements rather than focusing exclusively on GPU availability.

“We’ve always stated that we’re the tortoise in AI infrastructure,” he said.

Industry observers note that that approach reflects a broader change in how enterprises are approaching AI. Early infrastructure demand largely came from hyperscalers, AI research organizations and startups building large-scale models. Those customers needed access to GPU clusters, often through bare-metal infrastructure.

Industry observers note that the next phase is different. Enterprises are looking to use AI agents to streamline operations, improve customer experiences and create newly introduced revenue opportunities. Those applications must work alongside existing enterprise systems, comply with security requirements and integrate with established network and application architectures.

Industry observers note that bare-metal GPU infrastructure alone does not address those needs. Cochrane identified complexity and a lack of specialized skills as major obstacles to enterprise AI adoption. Organizations may have access to powerful accelerators, but they still need the surrounding infrastructure and services to build, deploy and operate applications.

Industry observers note that vultr’s strategy is to provide a more integrated environment, including traditional cloud compute, GPU infrastructure, networking, storage and access to cloud-native projects. Cochrane stated the platform supports more than 60 Cloud Native Computing Foundation projects that customers can deploy directly.

Industry observers note that the goal is to reduce the work required to assemble an AI environment. Rather than making enterprises integrate every component themselves, providers can offer preconfigured services and composable infrastructure that developers can deploy as needed.

That distinction is becoming notable as AI moves beyond experimentation. Enterprises need infrastructure that supports production applications, not just model training and inference.

It has been revealed that the growing focus on GPUs has sometimes obscured the role of traditional computing resources in AI architectures. But agentic AI is expanding the range of workloads that infrastructure providers must support.

According to recent reports, an AI agent does more than send a prompt to a model and receive a response. It may execute scripts, interact with repositories, run builds, access databases and invoke external tools. Those activities require compute resources beyond the GPU.

“Not all workloads need to be on a GPU,” Cochrane said.

Recent findings suggest that CPUs remain essential for databases, application code and data pipelines. They can also support smaller, optimized open-source models and inference workloads that do not require dedicated accelerators.

Another emerging requirement is the environment in which agents execute tasks. As agents gain the ability to run code and interact with systems, enterprises need secure sandboxes that isolate those activities from production environments and sensitive resources.

Cochrane pointed to work underway in the cloud-native ecosystem around safe and secure agent sandboxes as an indication of how infrastructure requirements are changing.

This creates a more complex infrastructure model. GPUs may handle demanding model reasoning and inference, while CPUs support the applications, pipelines and execution environments surrounding those models.

For organizations, the implication is that enterprise AI infrastructure decisions should account for the entire agentic workflow. Buying GPU capacity without considering the compute, storage, networking and isolation requirements around it can create another infrastructure silo. A full-stack approach gives platform teams more flexibility to match resources to individual workloads while maintaining a consistent operational environment.

As enterprises expand AI deployments across regions, data sovereignty is becoming more than a question of where information is stored.

Organizations operating in regulated industries or under national data requirements need to understand where data resides, which services can access it and what happens if infrastructure outside a particular region becomes unavailable.

Cochrane described Vultr’s regional architecture as an isolation model in which each of its 34 global data center regions operates independently. According to him, data within a region remains resident there and is not accessed by Vultr services outside that region.

Sources indicate that the distinction extends beyond data residency to application operations. Cochrane used France as an example. An application running in a French region should continue operating even if Vultr’s global control plane and its other regions become unavailable.

“If the rest of the world went dark, your production application in France? It just runs,” he stated.

Industry observers note that that approach is intended to reduce dependencies on global services that could otherwise affect regional application availability. It also gives organizations a clearer boundary for managing sensitive workloads and maintaining operational continuity.

Recent findings suggest that for enterprises, this is an important architectural consideration. A cloud provider may offer regional data storage, but that does not necessarily mean every service required to operate an application is isolated within the same geography.

As AI applications become more deeply integrated into business operations, organizations will need to evaluate sovereignty across the full application stack, including data, compute, management services and operational dependencies.

The cost of running AI applications is becoming another major consideration as organizations move from pilots to sustained production workloads.

Inference costs can increase quickly when agents repeatedly call models, retrieve information and execute multi-step workflows. As usage grows, enterprises must balance model performance, throughput and infrastructure expense.

Cochrane believes some organizations will increasingly turn to open-source models that can be adapted to their own data and operated on infrastructure they control. Rather than relying entirely on large commercial models for every task, enterprises can post-train specialized models using proprietary information and deploy them for operational workloads where that approach makes sense.

He described an example involving a platform engineering organization that reduced inference costs by 80% by post-training an open-source model and running it on its own infrastructure. The example illustrates a potential economic advantage, although results will depend on the workload, model, infrastructure and operational requirements involved.

Industry observers note that the broader point is that organizations are beginning to evaluate the economics of enterprise AI infrastructure across the entire stack. Model selection matters, but so do infrastructure utilization, throughput, data movement and the cost of operating agents over time.

For some workloads, owning more of the infrastructure and model lifecycle may provide better cost control than depending entirely on external inference services.

Sources indicate that that does not mean every enterprise should build and operate its own models. It does suggest that organizations need more flexibility to choose where models run and how workloads are distributed.

The changing infrastructure requirements of agentic AI are also expanding the responsibilities of platform engineering teams.

Cochrane expects platform engineers to become central to enterprise AI adoption, working more closely with business units to understand which agents and preconfigured application environments are needed across the organization.

That moves platform engineering beyond infrastructure provisioning and developer enablement. Teams will increasingly need to help define the building blocks that allow developers to deploy governed AI applications without having to assemble every component independently.

According to recent reports, cochrane also sees an opportunity for the cloud-native community to evolve how it shares infrastructure patterns. The CNCF ecosystem has helped developers adopt individual open-source projects across networking, storage, observability and other infrastructure categories. But as architectures become more complex, organizations need guidance on how those components fit together.

It has been revealed that cochrane predicted the emergence of marketplaces where developers can share opinionated, prebuilt stacks for specific workload types. Instead of selecting and configuring individual components, teams could start with a tested architecture and adapt it to their requirements. That could help reduce the complexity of building agentic applications while encouraging more consistent deployment practices.

Recent findings suggest that he also expects consolidation in the neocloud market. Providers focused primarily on bare-metal GPU capacity may face pressure as enterprises demand broader cloud capabilities. Those able to expand into full public cloud platforms could be better positioned to serve production workloads.

Vultr’s existing cloud platform gives it a foundation for that transition, Cochrane remarked, with its investments in both traditional compute and specialized AI infrastructure.

Enterprise AI is changing the definition of cloud infrastructure. GPUs remain key, but agentic applications require a broader foundation that includes CPUs, secure execution environments, networking, storage, data sovereignty and integrated cloud-native services.

It has been revealed that that creates an opportunity for providers that can deliver more than specialized accelerator capacity. It also puts platform engineering teams in a more strategic position as enterprises work to standardize how AI applications are built, deployed and governed.

The next phase of the neocloud market may therefore be determined less by who can offer the most GPU capacity and more by who can provide the complete environment enterprises need to run AI in production.

Recent findings suggest that as Cochrane’s comments suggest, the infrastructure challenge is no longer simply making AI compute available. It is making the entire system around AI practical to operate at enterprise scale.

(Trace) has been awarded a position on Support Area 3 (SA3): Cloud, Infrastructure, & Cybersecurity Services of the General Services Administration (GSA) Technology Transformation Services (TTS) Next-Generation IT Solutions (NEXT) Blanket Purchase Agreement (BPA). This five-year BPA, awarded under the GSA Alliant 3 Governmentwide Acquisition Contract, has no ceiling value across its life. These capabilities will enable federal agencies to modernize legacy environments, strengthen cybersecurity postures, and improve the reliability and performance of critical technology systems.

"This award is an important step in Trace's continued growth and expands our ability to bring proven technical capabilities to a broader range of federal customers," said Stacey McGill, Vice President of Enterprise Solutions. "We look forward to supporting the acceleration of technological modernization and delivering solutions that enable Government agencies to operate more effectively.".

This award is underpinned by Trace's proven expertise in provisioning secure infrastructure, cloud technologies, and cybersecurity services for Government customers. It cements Trace's position as one of the first contractors to receive an award on Alliant 3.
